speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING
(Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, I have again to ask the house to pause in its proceedings to permit mention being made of the sudden passing of another of our number, who but a few days ago was in his accustomed seat, to all appearances in the best of health. I refer to Mr. Alexander McKay Edwards, the deputy whip of the conservative opposition, who for nearly thirteen years past has represented the constituency of South Waterloo in this house.
At the end of the week before last, when the hon. the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) left Ottawa to address a meeting in the city of Galt, Ontario, in the constituency of the hon. member, the minister was accompanied by Mr. Edwards, who on the day following introduced him to his audience. Later in the day Mr. Edwards complained of not feeling well, and was obliged to rest. It was not thought, either by himself or by others, that his condition was serious. On Friday last this house had only begun its afternoon's proceedings when word was received that the hon. membei had passed away.
Mr. Edwards was in his sixty-third year. He was born at Bothwell, Ontario, but at an early age went to live in Waterloo county. His personal, business and political interests were centred in the county of Waterloo, and, more particularly, in and about the thriving and industrial communities of Galt and Preston. His career, however, had its intimate association with the affairs of his native province and with the larger and wider interests of our dominion.
By marriage, Mr. Edwards was related to the late Hon. George Clare who for many years represented the constituency of South Waterloo in this parliament. Like the late George Clare, Mr. Edwards held an enviable place in the esteem and confidence of his fellow citizens. He was successful and prominent in business; the head of an important manufacturing enterprise, and the director of several others. For eight years he served the city of Galt as an alderman, and for two years as its chief magistrate. He was first elected to the House of Commons in the general election of 1925, and was reelected at each of the three subsequent general elections, representing the constituency in all, as I have said, for nearly thirteen years.
During his years in parliament, Mr. Edwards represented his constituents with fidelity and ability. He was held in high personal esteem in parliament as he was in his constituency. In this house he was regular in his attendance, was active in the work of its committees. When he participated in the debates he spoke to the point, and was listened to with attention and respect. As assistant to the chief whip of the Conservative party, he rendered services which were much appreciated by all parties in the house.
It is not without significance that his last public act should have been the one to which I have already alluded, an act of courtesy and chivalry towards a political opponent. It was the expression of a nature which was essentially kindly, cheerful, and generous, and which won for him many strong and enduring friendships among members of all parties.
We shall all greatly miss his pleasing personality. His was a career of quiet, unobtrusive conscientious service to his community and to his party, one which maintained and served to further the amenities of public and parliamentary life. Not his party only, but the entire membership of this house, has suffered in his passing a loss which will be deeply felt.
I extend to hon. gentlemen opposite, and to their leader, the very sincere sympathy of my colleagues and myself, and, indeed, of all hon. members on this side, in the loss of so old, trusted, loyal, and valued a colleague and friend.
I should like to express our sympathy as well to the constituency which the late member represented so faithfully over many years.
To Mrs. Edwards, and to her son and daughter, who have been thus greatly bereaved, and to the aged mother of Mr. Edwards, who shared his household and now mourns the loss of her son, the sympathy of all hon. members of this house goes out in fullest measure. It would, Mr. Speaker, be appreciated by all if this expression of our sympathy could be conveyed by Your Honour, to Mrs. Edwards, and to the other members of the family.

Mr. Speaker, may I first thank the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for his kindly sympathetic and appreciative references to the gentleman whose loss we mourn to-day, one who was a prominent member of the official opposition. The house meets under the shadow of death of one of its members. This has happened so frequently during the present parliament that we are reminded of the saying that there is nothing certain about man's life but this, that he shall lose it.

Questions

As has been ably pointed out by the Prime Minister, the late Mr. Edwards by his activities in his home town and constituency was well qualified to be a worthy representative of that constituency in the House of Commons. He became a member in 1925, and since that time has continuously represented South Waterloo. His membership in the house was characterized by regularity of attendance, industry, careful attention to his many duties in the house and to the deliberations of the important committees upon which he served. His zeal for his constituency was outstanding, and the confidence of his electors was expressed as has been indicated here. Although his speeches in the house were not frequent, they showed careful preparation and a knowledge of his subject, and were delivered in a calm and reasoned manner which commanded respect, carried conviction, and made a lasting impression upon his hearers. His relations with his fellow members were cordial, and in a large measure he enjoyed their confidence.
The sympathy which will go out from this house and from the large number of people who knew the Late Mr. Edwards will in a measure help to sustain his mother, his widow and family in their sad bereavement. With the right hon. leader of the official opposition and hon. members supporting him I join in requesting that Your Honour convey to them our expression of deep sympathy.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to associate myself with what has been said respecting our late colleague, Mr. Edwards. I am sure it will be consoling to his family to know of the high esteem in which he was held by members of the house. In my association with him I always looked upon him as a kindly and generous man, one who had no hate in him. Such characteristics in these days are in certain quarters no longer regarded as virtues, and it is well that we lay special emphasis upon them. With the other members of the group to which I belong, I wish to associate myself with what has been so well said by those who have preceded me.

Mr. Speaker, the group to which I belong wishes to associate itself with the expression of appreciation of services rendered and sympathy for the bereaved. When we met the late brother in the lobbies and through the Various activities of the house, we learned to respect and honour him. With other hon. members who have spoken we would request you, Mr. Speaker, to convey our sympathy to the bereaved family.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTENTION TO PROCEED WITH LEGISLATION AT THE PRESENT SESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, based on considerable correspondence, and also on copies of petitions I have received, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I have been urged, and I have no doubt other hon. members have been, to support a measure, promised in the speech from the throne, which would set up in Canada a system of unemployment insurance. Will the Prime Minister inform the house whether he is
likely to bring down such a measure during the present session? Perhaps he has a general statement to make in the matter; if so, I believe the country would be pleased to hear it at this time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTENTION TO PROCEED WITH LEGISLATION AT THE PRESENT SESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the moment I am unable to recall the exact words which appear in the speech from the throne. So far as I recollect however they were to the effect that the government hoped to be in a position, through the cooperation of the several provinces, to bring in a national unemployment insurance measure. It has been understood from the outset that in the opinion of the administration a scheme of national unemployment insurance is the one which would be most in the interests alike of the provinces and the dominion. For that reason it has been hoped that the dominion would have the hearty cooperation of the provinces in permitting an amendment to the British North America Act which would give this parliament full jurisdiction with respect to the enactment of unemployment insurance. The hon. member who has just spoken, and no doubt all other hon. members of the house, know that the government has not received from some of the provinces endorsa-tion of the view that this parliament should be given power to enact an unemployment insurance measure. We are still hoping that in this matter the reasons which may be actuating the provinces referred to will be further considered and that ultimately all will see the wisdom of cooperating in a national unemployment insurance measure. However, it is not the intention of this government to seek to coerce the provinces with respect to any legislative measure which is in the nature of a social service measure. Our aim rather is to be helpful and to further if we can mutual interests. We do not want to appear, let alone in reality, to seek in any way to coerce any province of the dominion. It would look at the moment as though it will not be possible to get that cooperation with respect to unemployment insurance before the present session comes to its close, but if it should be obtained the measure will be introduced.
The reference to this matter in the speech from the throne was as follows:
The cooperation of the provinces has been sought with a view to an amendment of the British North America Act, which would empower the parliament of Canada to enact forthwith a national scheme of unemployment insurance. My ministers hope the proposal may meet with early approval, in order that unemployment insurance legislation may be. enacted during the present session of parliament..

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I gather that the purpose of the minister and of the government in introducing this legislation has been to assist in the relief of unemployment. Unemployment is most severe in several of the larger cities, and the bill contains a provision limiting a loan to any one of those municipalities according to the municipality's population in proportion to that of the rest of the dominion. I am inclined to think that in some respects that provision will defeat the purposes of the legislation, because the smaller municipalities that might desire to take advantage of it and come under its provisions have probably no great number of unemployed. For example, in a town of ten or twenty thousand or a city of fifty thousand there may not be many unemployed, but such municipalities come within the scope of this legislation. On the other hand, in Montreal there are probably one to one and a quarter million people in the city and surrounding suburbs; under this provision they would get for all that area possibly only one-tenth of this appropriation. So many of the smaller municipalities will desire or need to take advantage of the legislation that it seems to me a considerable amount of this money will not be employed if you impose this limit upon it. The whole of this money cannot be expended under the plan of thi3 legislation unless every municipality takes advantage of it.

When the bill first

I am not in a position to gauge the extent of the objections which reached the minister, nor have I had the opportunity of following in detail the proceedings before the committee. Would the minister give a short statement with regard to the principle of agreed charges, and deal particularly with what seemed to be an indication that people who disagreed with the agreed charges were of the opinion that the charges, would be secret and that information as to details of arrangements would not be available.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
The principle of agreed
charges is that the railways shall have the power, under conditions including wide publicity, to make a contract with a shipper to carry all or part of his goods at a special rate to be agreed upon. The conditions are these. If the railway and the shipper reach an agreement, such agreement is submitted for approval to the board of transport commissioners. That body in turn under the provisions of the bill must publish in the Canada Gazette a synopsis of the proposed agreement and give it as wide publicity as they would give the setting of a new rate. In other words they notify every important trade body and all important associations of shippers, boards of trade, chambers of commerce and municipalities affected by the charge. They give to the agreement what they have found by experience to be the widest possible publicity. Thirty days later a hearing is held at which any shipper or body of shippers or carrier under the act may appear before the board and make objection to the agreement, urging that it may be dis-

Transport Commission
criminatory in some way or would unduly injure the business of some shipper or carrier. When the agreement is made it must be made immediately available to any firm operating under substantially similar conditions. That is, if another firm is willing to agree to substantially the same provisions as to all or part of its freight, it is entitled to the same agreement. There is a provision that the rate shall be the same for one as for more than one carload. Other provisions, which will appear as we study the bill, stipulate that these agreements shall not be used to favour the large shipper as against the small shipper. The provisions are somewhat narrower than those of the British bill because rates must be quoted in cents per pound. The British bill permits a somewhat wider latitude in the making of agreed rates. In some cases the rate is a percentage of the gross value of shipments, but in this part the rate is restricted to a rate in cents per pound. A provision is also included that the agreed charges made by one railway are open to the other railways.

I understand a number

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Only the bulk carriers.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Did not the Canadian
Manufacturers' Association object?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Yes, they filed an objection.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
The minister seems quite
clear in his mind that this legislation will work out reasonably and without undue delay. However, the procedure seems to be somewhat lengthy. The bill has been before a committee upon which was represented all the parties and we can only hope that it will work out as the minister suggests it will. There is one phase of this bill which I have not yet heard explained. Sometimes an argument can be made to better advantage when a concrete case is given rather than by theorizing. I should like to outline a situation that exists on the coast. There is competition, rather onesided I should think, between the shipping and rail companies in connection with the shipment of lumber from British Columbia. It is apparent that this competition must be very onesided, because it is much cheaper to ship lumber by water through the Panama canal than by rail. It has been suggested that the shipments by water are comparatively trivial, but I do not think that is the fact. A service of one and a half, so to speak, or two boats a month is maintained. The company do not necessarily own all these boats, but they charter the necessary boats to maintain their schedule. They have captured trade for our lumber people in British Columbia which would be utterly lost if they had to depend on the railways. Here is the picture that is presented, and if the minister can satisfy the people for whom I am speaking I shall be very glad. The railway board has authority to make cut-throat rates over a given period, and evidently that is the intention. Well, they make those cut-throat 
rates, and after they have been in force for six months or a year the shipping companies will be driven out of business, not being able to meet those rates. The net result will be that the lumber shipper in British Columbia, when the boat companies have been put out of business, will have no recourse except to use the railways, and it will be impossible to use the railways because of the necessarily high rates. We have a substantial market on the Atlantic coast, both in Canada and in the United States, which we may be in danger of losing under this legislation, and it will not benefit the railways either because once they have driven the shipping companies out of business and then have raised their own rates again, our lumber people will not be able to use the railways, and in that way we will be deprived of a very useful market, although perhaps not a very big one. If the minister will explain how that danger is to be obviated I shall be very much interested in his explanation.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: How much lumber does British Columbia ship by rail?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Perhaps not very much unless they ship it to the prairies, which it is impossible to reach by boat. They cannot ship by rail to the east because of the high rates, and that is the danger I am pointing out.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Where are your markets for shipments by rail?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: The only rail market available to us now is the prairies. The danger is that the railways will take this eastern business away from the shipping people by means of cut-throat rates, and then having put the shipping companies out of business, they will raise railway rates again and we will lose our Atlantic seaboard market which we have in Canada and the United States.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: By water?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Yes, by water, and we want to maintain that market by water. We do not want water competition put out of business by a temporary cut-throat rate from the railways.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: British Columbia products are practically all shipped by water.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Not entirely.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Not entirely.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
British Columbia lumber is shipped to St. John by water. I know something about it. How much lumber do you sell in the maritimes that is shipped by rail?

Transport Commission

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
I should not imagine we
should ship any by rail to Saint John and we never will either. But if the railway companies are allowed by cut-throat rates to put water competition out of business, we shall be out not only rail traffic but the boat traffic which we now have and do not want to lose.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
I have had some experience in buying British Columbia lumber for use at eastern points, and the position is this, that if the lumber is needed for quick delivery it is forwarded by rail; if the buyer can wait two or three months for delivery, it is shipped by boat. There is a considerable difference in the rates, but I think at least fifty per cent of the lumber that goes into construction work in the east is shipped by rail. It is a matter of urgency. Ordinarily timber for heavy construction is cut to dimensions and forwarded for a certain work. I know in my own experience that in two cases out of three at least, we do not want to wait for delivery and so have shipments forwarded by rail-timber sheet piling, for instance. The rail rate is substantially higher, unquestionably, than shipment by vessel through the Panama canal.
But the position, Mr. Chairman, is this, that no one can be forced to make an agreed charge. An agreed charge is a voluntary affair, and if it is made it will be made because it is advantageous to the shipper as well as to the carrier. The lumber trade of British Columbia is very highly organized, particularly as to marketing, and I cannot believe that the lumber trade of British Columbia would make an agreed charge that would have the effect my hon. friend suggests. They would look far enough ahead to see that that might happen, and would get along without the agreed charge. However, I do not think the agreed charge is intended to operate in connection with a large commodity like lumber. I do not think any carrier would try to get all the lumber business of British Columbia by an agreed charge. I doubt if that is a case in point, and so far as the agreed charge is concerned I believe the effect on the lumber industry of British Columbia will be nil.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
I was a member of
the committee which considered the bill, and if I know anything about the bill at all it gives control to the board of transport commissioners. There is also a clause in the bill which definitely provides that railway companies in making agreed charges shall have due regard to the actual cost of moving freight. If the bill means anything, it will
be the function of the board of transport commissioners to see that the railways do not make agreements at rates that will be less than the actual cost of handling freight, and if the terms of the bill are carried out in that respect there is no chance in the world of the railways veiy seriously undercutting the boat companies.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Our worry is that the
shipping line or lines between British Columbia and eastern Canada will be put out of business. The great danger, as I see it, is that agreed charges may be made in the east on goods shipped from the east to British Columbia, making it temporarily cheaper to ship by rail than by water through the Panama canal, with the result that the shipping line would be put out of business. I believe that at present wre bring quite a lot of merchandise to British Columbia from eastern Canada by water cheaper than it can be brought in by rail, and the fact that there is that water competition has kept down railway rates on other goods that are not brought in by the ships at all. It is to preserve that situation that we are so anxious. Can the minister give us any assurance that agreed charges cannot be used to wipe out the business which at the present time is being carried by ship from eastern Canada through the Panama canal to the Pacific coast?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Does my hon. friend refer to liners or tramps? Tramps will always be available.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: There are no tramps. We have one line at the present time running a regular service from Montreal to the Pacific coast and back.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Which is it?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: I forget the name, but their office is in Montreal, and they have materially helped in keeping down freight rates on commodities going from eastern Canada not only to the Pacific coast, but from there into Alberta.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: My hon. friend's remarks would apply only to liners, because, except under abnormal conditions, there will always be a plentiful supply of tramps.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: There are no passenger liners between Vancouver and the east. There are freight liners.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
This is a
freight line with definite sailings.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Yes, that is what I was referring to-freight liners as distinguished from tramps.
Transport Commission

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
I do not think the last speaker was correct when he said there will be plenty of tramp steamers available. My impression is that the tramp steamer will have to go to the board of transport for a licence and will have to show that that service is required; and my fear is that they will not be able to procure a licence, and it will mean that the steamship line now in operation between Montreal and Vancouver will be the only one granted a licence. Any shipper wanting to ship by tramp steamer will have to advise that line to go to the .board of transport commissioners for a licence and must prove that there is not adequate transportation service either present or future.
Regarding the remarks of the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) I shall be delighted if the board of transport commissioners can find out exactly the cost of hauling freight. It is something I have been trying to get for a long time. I can tell him that the chief counsel of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company stated on oath that there is no one in the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian National or on this continent or any other who can tell exactly what it costs to haul goods by rail. How they will be able to compare the cost of hauling by rail with that of carriage by ships and by air I cannot understand.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: I feel that I can speak on this subject because I was born and brought up in the shipping business. I have brought many cargoes of Douglas fir from British Columbia and I can tell hon. members that Douglas fir is being shipped from Vancouver to Saint John to-day by water at $7 per thousand feet. The railways have no chance to compete with that; they cannot meet that price. It is all a matter of competition. How much lumber is shipped to eastern Canada from British Columbia by railway? I have seen cargo after cargo of Douglas fir from British Columbia at $7 per thousand delivered in Saint John, by way of steamers carrying 5,000,000 superficial feet.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
That is not what we are afraid of. Our fear is that there will be a wall placed around us so that no steamship companies can get in. That freight of which my friend speaks is business which would not be obtained by merchants in British Columbia but for the fact that the steamships are carrying it, because the railroad rate is roughly S27 per thousand feet. He is correct in saying that the railways will never be able to compete with the steamship lines, but tramp steamers and other steamers operating via the Panama canal are able at times to carry that business partly

because they have freight for United States Atlantic seaboard cities as well as Canadian cities. Having a full cargo made up in that way enables them to carry the business, but they will not be able to do so in the future if they are prevented from obtaining licences.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: It is well to bear in mind that the carrying of lumber from British Columbia to the Atlantic is only one side of the question; the other is the obtaining of return cargoes. A freight line must be sure it is going to get a return cargo. When this service was first established between Vancouver and the Atlantic ports the draft of the vessels, and the width likewise, was governed by the depth of the Laehine canal. I do not know what governs now, but four years ago that was very definite-the draft had to be not over seventeen feet, I think.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Fourteen feet.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Yes, I was not sure. They carry back from lake ports furniture, canned goods and similar freight. So both sides of the question have to be considered.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Once again I may say that the railways are in no different position from the boat lines. Any agreed charges the railways can make the boat lines can make. I cannot believe that one will seriously affect the other. Neither can afford to cut rates to an unprofitable level. I look for no wild rate cutting. In England this practice has developed slowly, it is now in I think, its fourth year. In the first year there were about thirty-three agreed charges made, and now I believe there are about two thousand outstanding. Careful investigation there shows that the carriers believe it has been helpful and the shippers believe it is helpful. Here I believe the history will be much the same; the agreed charges will be entered upon very cautiously and develop slowly, there will be no great rush to make agreed charges. I think there will be only a few at the start. But I can see no serious damage to any part of the shipping industry or to the carrying industry arising from agreed charges, considering all the safeguards thrown about the making of them in this bill.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Can the minister assure us
it is not the intention to give the railways power to put this shipping line out of business by means of agreed charges?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Yes, there are special provisions made against that sort of thing; there is a special section which deals with that. It cannot be used to put a competitor out of business.

Transport Commission

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
It is not the intention that
the railways shall have these agreed charges to use as a club over the shipping lines?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
The shipping lines have the
agreed charges just as have the railways. The only thing is that up to now the railways have been told to stand on a certain level, while all other carriers-motor trucks, ships-can go as much under that level as they like. The difference is that now the railways will not have to stand on that level.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: But the shipping is regulated also.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: The shipping can make agreed charges also.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
The minister says people
are not likely to cut prices below normal. But that is a common everyday thing. I will not advertise the firm by giving the name, but a firm came into a town with which I am familiar, went to the established dealer in their line, and said: We will give you so much for your business. The men demurred as to the amount. Well, he was told, we will come in and establish a branch and will put you out of business. It may cost us $2,000 or $10,000, but we will do it, because that is our established policy when we make up our minds to take possession of a certain town with our line; we do it regardless of the cost, and we do it with a certain amount of warning to other people not to be caught in the same way. The minister says that the lumber people in British Columbia who are well organized will not be so ill-advised as to patronize railway cut rates to the extent of putting the boat line out of business. That is probably true because they are closely knit and well organized. But as the hon. members for Nanaimo (Mr. Taylor) and Vancouver South (Mr. Green) have said, that line of boats cannot exist without return cargoes, and the return cargo consists of manufactured or package goods from the east.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Anything they can get.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
In other words they pick
over all the high grade freight from eastern Canada to get one boat load every six weeks.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
The eastern manufacturer does not know about this theory of the boat being put out of business, and would be quite indifferent to it anyway. The average person buys in the cheapest market, and if he is confronted with a lower rate on the railway he will take the lower one. He is not going to listen to this yarn, as he will call it, that if you do not deal with us we will
be put out of business. The result will be the imminent danger of that happening of which I spoke at first, that, perhaps deliberately, the price will be cut in order to put the boat out of business and then the higher railway rates will be restored. If it were only a question of people paying the higher rates, that would not matter so much perhaps from the point of view of the British Columbia producer, but it would mean to him that he would lose his market, because his market for a certain class of lumber in the Atlantic coast cities of the Unted States and Canada is dependent on his being able to ship by water at a low rate. The cargo is made up of goods partly in the United States and partly in Canada-partly one thing and partly another. It has not been satisfactorily explained to me, although I quite agree with the general principles of the bill and have supported the minister. I do see that danger, however, and the only hope that can be entertained is that it will not be effective in that regard, that is to say, that there will not be agreed charges on lumber. That is what the section is for, to allow a thing of that kind, and not to see that the board will prevent the railways from quoting a low price. But I see no provision that would prevent them from doing that; and as the hon. member for New Westminster has pointed out, what the exact cost of a certain freight is the railway companies themselves cannot say.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: As regards putting the boat line out of business or preventing freight from going west, this boat line goes all the way from the maritimes up the Bt. Lawrence and the great lakes as far as Hamilton and it takes whatever goods are offered at the most profitable freight that can be got. Unless all business in Canada were covered by agreed charges, how would it be possible to stop that boat from getting a return cargo, considering all the commodities that move from one coast to the other, without time being a great factor?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: The answer is that the elimination of the lumber traffic from British Columbia might make such a difference that they could not afford to operate profitably.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
But surely the lumber traffic of British Columbia would be the one business that agreed charges could never touch. In the first place it is too voluminous a traffic to trifle with; in other words, if any carrier made an agreed charge to handle all the lumber traffic at an unprofitable rate, or a
Transport Commission

rate that would take business away from the ships, that carrier would be bankrupt within twelve months.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
A representative of the
Canadian industrial traffic league appeared before the committee and made clear the reasons for objections to the regulations of the intercoastal water movement between Canadian Atlantic and Canadian Pacific ports. The reasons given were as follows:
1.	This service is different from other water services in that it is in direct competition with world-wide all water services, some of which are unregulated, and the Canadian intercoastal service would, therefore, be placed at a very great disadvantage if regulation of rate matters is insisted upon.
2.	This intercoastal service is designed to transport goods between Atlantic and Pacific ports to enable shippers to lay their merchandise down in competition with these world-wide water services.
3.	This world-wide competition means the movement of goods from the highly industrialized countries of Europe, the United Kingdom and the United States, whether produced at low wage rates due to low living costs or by means of mass production. It thus affords the keenest competition and this intercoastal service is designed to meet this situation due to its lower operating costs.
4.	This competition being very keen, decision has very often to be made and contracts entered into at one or two hours' notice, and cannot wait for the involved procedure necessary and required if the intercoastal rate matters are to be regulated. It, therefore, requires the most simple procedure within which it may operate and enable it to obtain the benefits of its inherent advantages.
Those reasons applying to that service are clear and require very serious consideration on the part of the board.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: I might point out that my hon. friend is now discussing a part of the bill which was passed last Friday.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: This is in regard to rates; it covers agreed rates.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Those extracts relate to part II rather than part V.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Assuming that the agreed charge is filed and approved by the board and then it is desired by the organization that has entered into the agreement to have the charge increased; what is to be done?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: I do not quite get the question-increase what?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
The charge. Suppose
one carrier comes in and files an agreed charge-

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: An agreed charge is a contract.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: -and comes back in six months with a request to have that charge increased?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: An agreed charge is a contract between the carrier and the shipper for a certain definite period and at certain definite rates, and it is binding, like any other contract in law.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: It is only a contract.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: It is binding for the term of the contract and the board has no authority to terminate it or grant relief from it.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: It can be reviewed after one year on the application of either party.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
If the contract is for
five years, do I understand the minister to say that one of the parties may appear before the board and say, "Notwithstanding that we have a contract for five years we want it reviewed, we want a revision of it. It is true that we have not agreed upon any alteration in these charges, but we want you to review it."

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
I would refer the hon. member to subsection 9 of section 35, page 13:
AVhere the board has approved an agreed charge without restriction of time:
(a)	any shipper who considers that his business has been unjustly discriminated against as a result of the making ot the agreed charge,
(b)	any representative body of shippers, and
(c)	any carrier,
may, at any time after the expiration of one year from the date of the approval, apply to the board for the withdrawal of its approval of the agreed charge, and, upon any such application, the board may withdraw, or refuse to withdraw, its approval, or may continue its approval subject to such modifications being made in the charge as it thinks proper and as the carrier and the shipper to whose goods the charge is applicable are prepared to agree to:
I think that gives any party, even the party to the contract, the privilege of appearing before the board after one year to have the charge re-examined.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: That is a case where there is a charge agreed upon without limit as to the time for its operation. They just say, "We have agreed upon such a charge", and that is good for the year; and after the year it can be varied.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: That is the effect of it.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
If two parties make a contract for a definite period no one can interfere with it, but it is always open to an

Transport Commission
outside party to object to the agreed charge on the ground that it discriminates against his own business.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: I was a member of the committee that considered this bill and unfortunately, owing to the meeting of two or three other committees at the same time, I was unable to attend its sittings regularly. I do know, however, that there was a good deal of opposition to this part of the bill, and I am going to suggest to the minister that, as the leader of the opposition desires to make some observations upon it, he allow this part to stand, or at least some section of it, in order that an opportunity may be presented of discussing the matter from the standpoint of the objections that have been raised. I am not in a position to enter into that discussion to-day. As regards the part dealing with harbour tolls, there are one or two members who have some objections to raise, but they are not here to-day. Possibly the minister would make as much progress if he would allow these parts to stand and take them up again.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: I should like to pass as many clauses as possible to-day in order to get the bill over to the other chamber; at least we have been requested to get it over there as soon as possible, in order that that chamber may have the necessary time to examine it. I think the leader of the opposition knew that this bill was coming up to-day and made no objection to its being considered. Would it satisfy my hon. friend if we left one subsection open?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: As long as it is left open with that understanding. I am not sure that there will be any amendments suggested, and I have no objection to passing upon these sections, with such suggestions as we may wish to make, leaving one section open upon which a general discussion of this part may take place. That would be quite satisfactory. I should think the first subsection would be the one to leave open, because that launches the whole proposition.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Then I would ask that subsection 1 of section 35 be allowed to stand.
Subsection stands.
Subsections 2 and 3 agreed to.
On section 35, subsection 4

Board approval of agreed charge.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
I notice that this is retroactive in its operation; it says:
-from which it shall be deemed to have become operative, shall be such date, not being 51952-227
earlier than the date on which application for approval was lodged, as may be fixed by the board.
Is the effect of that to make the rate retroactive to the date of the application, though it may not be approved until some considerable time later?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, I should like to say a few words in reference to a matter which has been drawn to the attention of this house on a number of occasions during the past few weeks. I refer to a situation which has existed in Vancouver since the end of April and which became acute during the latter part of May. A number of single unemployed men took possession of certain buildings in that city, including the post office and the art gallery, and after eighteen days these men are still in possession of those buildings. I have tried, along with other hon. members, to impress upon the government the fact that if this situation is not remedied serious trouble will result. We believe that something could have been done to prevent this situation from arising, and we believe that something should be done immediately to try to arrive at a settlement of the problem before trouble occurs. These men are being provided with food which indicates to me that in a large measure they have the sympathy of the people of Vancouver. Being confined in such cramped quarters, these men undoubtedly will become irritable and trouble is likely to be the result. Conditions in British Columbia and Vancouver are not as good to-day as they were even a year ago. I have before me a letter from the mayor of Vancouver under date of May 31, from which I should like to read briefly in order to show just what is the unemployment situation in that city. He said.
The employment situation in the city of Vancouver is not quite as good as it was last year at this time. We have not had the usual

spring pick-up of work. The logging camps are not working at the same capacity they were last year and the pulp and paper mills have curtailed their output very materially causing reduction in their working time, in some instances close to half time.
As you are aware we had the usual drift to the coast last fall of quite a group of men from other parts of Canada who were taken care of by the provincial and dominion governments through the forestry camps and following their usual custom they have closed them for the summer. Usually a great many of those in the camps left the province to return to the northwest for spring work while the remainder generally succeeded in getting something to do in the province on the road work which the provincial government generally inaugurated.
Unfortunately nothing has been done along that line this year as the premier seems to have been unable to make any arrangements for a loan from the dominion as in former years.
And further:
The unfortunate part to those purely British Columbia men is, pending cleaning up of the situation with the men on the sit-down strike, nothing can be done for the former which makes the situation here still more difficult for the municipal authorities. I cannot see for the life of me why the dominion government, realizing that this situation develops every spring, does not tackle it in an independent manner and establish a program of public works to take up the slack which private enterprise and industry do not seem able to absorb. Surely by this time after all of the representations w'hich have been made to them they should realize that this is more or less of a permanent problem and should be dealt with as such, in place of having this turmoil each spring and fall.
I think the mayor puts very clearly the reason why the men have at the present time the support of a great majority of the people of Vancouver. There is no opportunity of employment for these men. They are all employable unemployed under the age of fifty-five and are at the present time refused relief in that city.
I wish to say again, as I said a week ago, that if trouble develops in Vancouver the responsibility must be laid on the doorstep of this government. The circumstances are deplorable and are not at all in line with what was promised by this government in the compaign preceding the last general election. The present Prime Minister, speaking in Vancouver on July 31, 1935, promised:
Immediate abolition of the relief camps, and handling of the unemployment problem on a national basis, utilizing in adequately paid work of social value to the nation, those now unemployed.
These men now unemployed in Vancouver want that pledge of the Prime Minister carried out, and I feel satisfied that they would not be very insistent or particular as to the conditions under which they would work, but

they do want some kind of employment that will give them a livelihood. At the present time they have not that employment, and there is no prospect of their getting it.
On the same date, and during the same speaking engagement, the present Prime Minister said:
You have had one experience of being deceived by promises at a general election. Are you prepared to risk another? You have seen how long a period of time five years is-what opportunity it affords a ministry, if the ministry be so inclined, altogether to ignore, and even to defy, your clearly expressed will, and your most evident wishes.

I do not intend to thresh over old straw; but in justice to the men concerned and the citizens of greater Vancouver I feel that certain facts should be stated, facts which were not disclosed in previous discussions in this house. It is not an easy matter to discuss, but it is much more unpleasant to anticipate reports of still more disagreeable occurrences in Vancouver. Some of us who have lived there have witnessed disturbances on previous
occasions, and it is with dread that I pick up the morning newspapers now, lest I read the report of some serious trouble. The results of these disturbances were fully reported on former occasions. I have seen blood flow in the streets of Vancouver; I have seen people ridden down; I have seen men beaten up; I have seen inexcusable brutality exercised to deal with situations of this sort, and I would not be doing my duty did I not state in this house that which I have learned from reports reaching me daily now. A few days ago we did not have the information that we now have. One stubborn ugly fact stares us in the face, and cannot be disregarded. The men are without food and shelter. That was not disclosed before, because from the statement of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) we gathered that the deferred pay vouchers had been distributed in such a way that the men might carry on. On the minister's admission in the house the other day, however, the last distribution of pay vouchers took place on May 15, and I understand that no individual received more than $4 at that time.
These men are in a state of utter destitution; they are without food and shelter and without the means to move around and, as we say, " rustle " for work at any other point. You cannot expect men with empty bellies to face a situation of this kind in a calm and rational way. That must be understood. They feel desperate and they are likely to resort to desperate means to bring their predicament to the attention of the public. They are not, as has been implied, in a state of revolt against constituted authority. They feel they are engaged in a spectacular demonstration of the fact that authority as constituted in this country has denied them the elementary rights of livelihood.
May I quote their own statement appearing in what is known as the Post Office "Sit-downer's" Gazette, which is published by the men themselves with the aid of friends for the purpose of raising funds. They say:
This paper is not published or paid for by the Department of Labour or the government of British Columbia.
This is the statement I wish to read:
Please do not think that we do not fully realize the gravity of the situation we are facing. We know that this is one of the most serious problems that has ever faced the people and the government of Canada. We were forced to use this unusual method of bringing our case before you, the jury, when all constitutional means had been exhausted and the government and local authorities refused to act.
We ask that you base your verdict_ upon considerations of common humanity and justice and upon the actions of the boys themselves

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
which are all in accordance with peace and democracy. We are not a mob but a body of organized men with a very definite purpose, namely, to attain the status of Canadians with a chance to live a decent, human life.
We assure you that your property is safe in our hands. We, who are the workers and builders, without whom you would not have structures such as the art gallery and the post office, would be the last to injure or destroy that which cur hands have created. We thank you for your loyal and generous support of our cause. We realize that without you our attempt to secure justice would be a complete failure. Your moral support will be the surest guarantee that all Canadian youth will enjoy a future worthy of a country which has such noble traditions of democracy and which is rich in all that should make life a thing of enduring happiness and prosperity.
That indicates the attitude of the men, and if they resort to desperate tactics there are provocative conditions leading up to such action. We should look behind the existing disorder, as some might term it, and consider the conditions that led up to the action of the men. They did exhaust every lawful means of presenting their serious plight to the authorities and were denied redress, and they have merely taken a spectacular way of bringing their problem to the attention of the people of Canada.
The second ugly fact is this, that not all of these men in Vancouver are non-resident transients nor should be so described. I am advised, on the statement of a responsible member of the Vancouver council, that approximately fifty per cent of them under existing regulations may claim domicile in British Columbia. That means that there is going on behind the scenes the usual passing the buck between provincial and federal authorities. I have been through it and I know exactly what it means-the provincial authorities trying to capitalize the situation in order to secure greater aid from the federal authorities, and the federal authorities disclaiming all responsibility and publicly announcing that they are relying upon provincial government advice. I have been through such negotiations in the past and I know just what they mean. The men have fallen between two stools and the citizens of Vancouver are now facing the grief. The civic authorities of Vancouver and district are playing their part. They now accept full responsibility for relief of the unemployables. Under a recent classification they have the full burden of the unemployables. But in addition to that they are extending relief to single employable men over fifty-five. They are extending relief to veterans over fifty years of age. As regards the mining and forestry training schemes for young men, they are receiving applications only from those between the ages
[Mr. MacNeil.l
of eighteen and twenty-five, so that no administration of relief is being carried on by the provincial government for single unemployed between the ages of -twenty-five and fifty-five as formerly.

speechtext: Would it be a correct inference from what the hon. gentleman has said that -the only expectation of work which these men have is work provided by governments?	,

speechtext:
No; that is not their only expectation; but I will come to that point in a moment. They are not presented with any opportunities for employment in any quarter, and I intend to deal with that. The city has met the situation as well as it possibly can with the resources at its command and is carrying a heavy burden in this regard.
The third point is that raised by the minister. These men have not been presented with opportunities to secure employment, and in their present mood you cannot stave them off with vague generalities about employment in the distant future. They need employment immediately in order to obtain meals to-morrow and the next day. A man who has not a postage stamp or street ear fare cannot be put off with promises of something in the future. Before these men moved into the post office and art gallery they took pains to secure information as to employment opportunities across the prairies, and they received word from all the municipal bodies with whom they communicated that there were already local unemployed whose needs could not be met.
