After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Before the dinner recess I was attempting to explain wherein we were dealing with grievances distinctly different from those which were discussed on a former occasion. I refer to the fact that since the situation concerning the single unemployed in Vancouver was last discussed, approximately two hundred men have been arrested on a technical charge of obstructing the police in the performance of their duties. A number of them have been sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment ranging up to three months. Some have been released on their own recognizance under suspended sentence, and the cases of others have been adjourned because social service agencies have assured the court that in some manner they will be given food and shelter temporarily. Further, the men are

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
attempting to solicit alms on the street corners, holding out tin cans to passers-by as has been their custom on former occasions. Not all of these men are being arrested, but in every instance the funds contributed by the public of Vancouver are being confiscated and are not being made available for the benefit of the men, and thereby their situation is being rendered more desperate.
A new feature in the situation is this, that there is some evidence of lawlessness which was not apparent before, lawlessness which has been dealt with very fimly by the men themselves. On one or two occasions men in the art gallery have suggested that they should slash or cut valuable works of art in that building, and these men have been forcibly and promptly ejected by the other men. Another grievance, and one that affects the citizens at large, is that since of necessity the police reserves are concentrated in the centre of the city where the unemployed are congregated, outlying districts complain of a minor crime wave, and lawlessness is evident there with which the police are unable to cope.
This, I submit, Mr. Speaker, presents a situation entirely different from that which was discussed previously. I attempted to show that we must understand the psychology of these men in order to deal adequately with the situation. Hungry men are very much like cornered animals. After all, they are not made of very different stuff from the rest of us: the instinct of self-preservation is still alive, and I think it is to their credit that they have shown enough spirit to organize. While we may not find it possible to condone the means they have employed, at least, as I have said, they have shown sufficient spirit to bring their case to the attention of the public in a spectacular way. This must be said of the situation, that previously they did make representations in a lawful and orderly way to the civic authorities and to representatives of the provincial government, explaining their plight. Had they not taken this action, absolutely no attention would have been paid to their need, and they would have been required to suffer in silence.
I further pointed out that the situation is obscured by the fact that some of these men, under existing regulations, may claim domicile in British Columbia. Some fifteen hundred of the three thousand men involved have a right to claim domicile in British Columbia. I endeavoured to show that the city had made provision for some; but while the provincial minister of labour, Hon. Mr. Pearson, has stated that British Columbia will care for her own, that statement does not square with the facts. It is simply a red herring across
the trail. There is a large number of men who can turn to no other authority than the province of British Columbia; and, as I say, the province is unable, or has made no effort up to this time, to meet the necessities of those who are without work and without shelter, and who have no opportunity of getting work.
Before the recess the minister asked me if the men were relying on the expectation of work being provided by the provincial or the federal government. I do not think they are making a point in that regard. They are looking for work, anywhere, any kind of work. I know' these men, and I speak of the situation feelingly. It is exactly similar to the situation which arose on previous occasions. The last time we had trouble in Vancouver I was requested by the men to appear on their behalf in the police court, which I was permitted to do by courtesy of the court. Each evening I interviewed the men individually in the cells of the Vancouver police station, and I took particular pains to find out their circumstances. Let me suggest to the minister that when a man is under arrest, in the police station, facing a serious charge in court, he is perhaps more likely to tell the truth than on any other occasion. Just before I came down to the chamber this evening I glanced at the notes I took in regard to some two hundred individual cases on that occasion, so I know some of the circumstances which go to make up the problem of these men described as single and homeless, a description which is stamped on their relief cards. I say we must understand the circumstances which led up to the situation in which the men find themselves to undertsand the action which they have taken to make known their needs.
The point has been made several times that their situation is due very largely to their own shiftlessness; that if they had displayed the initiative which many of us were expected to show in our earlier days, the problem would be much easier of solution. Not four blocks away from the Vancouver post office is the office of the Employment Service of Canada, a well equipped office with an adequate staff, not only possessing information with regard to employment needs in that city but with a bulletin service indicating employment needs or any labour shortage at all important points in British Columbia or, as a matter of fact, at any point touched by that service. In the ordinary course of events, when these men were released from the camps they would naturally apply for work and register with the employment service. Not only that; they have tramped

Unemployed, Men in Vancouver
down the "skid road," as we call it in Vancouver, where they might learn of work in logging camps; they have looked for work on the waterfront; they have written letters to friends at different points outside Vancouver, and after all this they have found no prospect of employment anywhere. As I stated, before they moved into the post office, the art gallery and the Georgia hotel, acting under the advice of his worship the mayor of Vancouver they took pains to telegraph to the principal municipalities across western Canada asking if work was available at any point. In response to every inquiry they received notice that in each municipality there was already a surplus of labour, and that the community could not absorb any additional single unemployed. They were made to realize in a very emphatic manner-

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Were these telegrams
sent before or after their refusal to accept the proposal of the provincial minister of labour?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
I understand the telegrams were sent by the men after they had been offered transportation to any destination in the western provinces.
May I add this: There are various organized bodies of responsible citizens in Vancouver interested in securing employment for these men. There is one such committee to which I should refer; that is, the committee of representative business men, associated with the various churches and the social service agencies, which takes a special interest in the problems of homeless men. These men know whereof they speak; they have gone through this experience on former occasions, and at the present moment these men are trying with all the energy they possess to find employment for those men in whom they are particularly interested, the men whom they think are of worth while calibre, worth salvaging from their present dilemma. But they cannot find work for them. Under normal conditions or even those of last spring, the constituency which I represent might be expected to absorb a number of these single unemployed in various seasonal industries. At the present time, as reports indicate, these industries are unable to take on any additional number of these men. The small logging operators, who are carrying on their operations with tractors, logging out small limits, pockets of timber that have been overlooked by the big operators, report that their bunkhouses are full or that for various reasons they have been forced to cease operations for the present, possibly on account of the fire hazard. At every point fishing boats 
are tied up. The pulp and paper industry has been working on a five day week for months, and is now working only half time. And so it goes. These are the reports from the various districts in the constituency which I represent, and which normally each spring would absorb quite a number of these men. The conditions are not, as stated by the minister, such as would enable the men to disperse and readily find employment at these various points.
Some reference has been made to the leadership which these men have accepted; that has been discussed in somewhat derogatory terms. There may be some truth in what the minister says in that respect; but may I point out whatever leadership is offered, these men would not accept it for twenty-four hours if they had opportunities for employment. They are not of that type. I know them. I have been present at their meetings, when they determined that leadership from among their own number, in a democratic way; where their own policies were determined in a democratic way; where they discussed ways and means of bettering their position in a proper and orderly manner. So I think it is idle to argue at this time that they have blindly submitted to leadership of a subversive nature. . Within a few hours of any definite assurance that they could get employment at any point, there would not longer be any serious situation in Vancouver. It requires simply that we face the facts and apply common sense.
I would urge the minister to accept responsibility in his own department for direct negotiations with representatives of the men. It is hardly good enough to stand on the dignity of governmental departments. We should take a little of the starch and red tape out of negotiations now being conducted. On a former occasion when we had serious trouble in Vancouver a delegation largely representative of the Vancouver churches went to Victoria to interview the Minister of Labour. It happened that among the group was one representative of the men, and that man was denied admittance to the minister's office. The minister said he would receive only citizens, the implication being that these men were not to be regarded as citizens.
On other occasions the unemployed single men turned out to assist in connection with serious slides which interrupted railway and telegraphic communication. Some were killed because of their inexperience with railway signals. But officials grumbled because they were required to attend inquests; they said,

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
"The sooner these men are killed off, the better." The men are made to feel that they are no longer being treated like human beings. They have a hunted feeling. Under the conditions which have existed, they have been kicked about from pillar to post.
The minister does not recognize the difficulty in connection with the offer of transportation. I was brought face to face with this aspect of their problem when I interviewed one man after another. When I informed a man in the cells that his worship would in the morning probably advise him that he would be offered transportation to some destination named by him-his home, or wherever he claimed domicile-the man would probably answer, "I cannot go back; my people are in terrible circumstances now. If I go home I am not eligible for relief, and I cannot - get work. They have told me there is no work, and I am not going back home to be a burden on my folks." Other men would refer to the situation in the drought area, and show how impossible it wras for them to return to certain sections. Other men were without homes, and had been informed definitely in communities in which they had registered that, having forfeited domicile, there would be no relief and no work for them. If they go back they know they are going back to the same experience they have endured before, simply to be faced with an order from the police of that town to move to the next. They spend one night in the local hoosegow under orders to leave town in the morning. That has been in recent years the experience of thousands of young men across Canada. They have been moved from town to town on order of the police.
It is not a question of bad leadership at this time. By reason of circumstances preceding this situation they have reached a state of mind which is sad .to contemplate, one in which they would rather go to gaol than endure that which they were required to endure previously. They have had the experience of living in box cars and in jungle camps, and of being hounded from town to town. They have told me of that. They have said, "We would rather take it here at the end of a policeman's baton; we would rather be knocked insensible on the streets of Vancouver, than to go back to the hopelessness of drifting about and searching for work about which they tell us, but which we can never find."

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: What advice did you give them?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
It was not my business on that occasion to give them advice. I was acting on their behalf, through the courtesy of the magistrate, to state the circumstances
to the magistrate. And let it be said to the honour of the magistrate and the chief of police that they stated quite frankly in open court that it was not a criminal but rather an unemployment problem. The same scenes are again being enacted every morning in the Vancouver police court. Each morning they call long lists of men, and rows of men are formed three deep across the court room, while the police magistrate attempts to deal with the situation. It makes a burlesque of court procedure. Of course the men plead not guilty, and the police officers are called to the box to outline the circumstances. The men take the box, after pleading not guilty, and then admit that the circumstances as stated by the police officer are substantially correct. The magistrate in a friendly and informed manner discusses their circumstances and makes inquiries as to what may be done about them. He must resort to various devices, and try to deal with the situation in the light of extenuating circumstances revealed.
At the present time the gaol capacity is being taxed, and serious consideration is being given to moving the men by force to Pier's island, formerly a concentration camp for the Doukhobors. Over three hundred men were arrested and sentenced .before. Two hundred have now been arrested and are awaiting sentence. It is not a question of improper leadership. The situation challenges the leadership of the Minister of Labour. If he could walk into the post office in Vancouver at this time, and persuade the men to leave that building and walk four blocks to the office of the Employment Service of Canada, what would happen? If each man registered and said he wanted work, what would he be told? The answer would be, " There is nothing for you to do; come back to-morrow." If they go to industrial firms anywhere around Vancouver, they receive the same answer, "No work; come back next week." That is the answer they have been getting, and that is the answer they will now get if they go to the very agency the administration of which is under the control of the minister. I say that the Employment Service of Canada is in touch with labour requirements in all parts of Canada, and has nothing to offer these men. I have known business men in the city of Vancouver spend hours on the telephone in communication with employers not only in and around the city of Vancouver, but in the company towns along the coast, to see if the executives in those concerns could take on at least a few of the men. But all that work has been in vain.
If with the facilities at their command they failed to secure employment for these men,

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
how can we point the finger of blame at the unemployed man who, without the price of a postage stamp, finds it impossible to get work? The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) has shown that public opinion to some extent is behind these men. They are subsisting to-day on charitable contributions from the people of Vancouver. Those contributions are made simply because the people know that there is cause for the situation, that the men have a legitimate grievance and that there is no work available for them. Those people know that the unemployed are willing to work, if they are given opportunities to work. They know, too, that many of the men are without proper clothes to engage in heavy manual work. They know, too, that if they are sent to Swift Current or Moose Jaw or Battleford, or any points in the prairie provinces, they will not get work immediately. They will not have the opportunity to make immediate contacts for employment, and being out of funds, immediately will be picked up as vagrants, and dealt with by the police.
The Vancouver dailies are not prone to overlook or to defend any action suggesting lawlessness. But the editorial writers in those dailies are aware that there is a cause for the present situation. In editorial after editorial -they have asked that some plan be initiated by the federal government. The following is a brief quotation from the Vancouver Sun of May 25, 1938:
Human memories, on the average, are unfortunately short. The people of Vancouver however have good cause to remember that these young men, or others like them, have been put to this miserable expedient time and again in these last few years.
On Saturday they had ample opportunity to observe that these men, most of them young but a few of them grey headed, were decent looking young fellows, capable and well set up. And, if they were given to thinking at all, they must have been appalled with the tragedy displayed before their eyes, of a generation going to waste. They should be serving their country. No doubt one and all would be willing to do so, given a pick and shovel or whatever tools they are capable of using.
The federal Micawber government has dillydallied long enough with this problem, a problem affecting every citizen, a problem of wasting resources of man power-more valuable than any natural resources we have in our forests, hills and fields.
That editorial appeared in a paper which has given support to this government. The Daily Province of May 30 contained the following:
Two front page headlines of the Daily Province last Saturday made strange juxtaposition. One said, speaking of Vancouver: "Army of Women Plan to 'Tin Can' for 'Sit-Downers'."

The other, speaking of parliament at Ottawa, said: 'TOO Millions for New Works." What sense could you make of those two statements, taken together?
You could make no sense of them. Nobody can make any sense of the condition which they describe. One of them meant that a thousand men had seized and occupied two public buildings of this city, in protest against the fact that they had no work and no other means of support. The other meant that the parliament of Canada was about to vote one hundred millions for "work, wages and business."
For ten days now Vancouver has been subjected to the humiliation and the ill advertisement of this crazy situation. For ten days the government at Ottawa has played discreditable politics about it, making stupid incantations to the effect that it supported the "policy of the provincial government."
For ten days the government at Victoria has stood upon its stubbornness, refusing to do anything for these men unless they will accept a scheme which would dump them off the railway at some prairie station where they may not be wanted and where there may not be anything for them to do.
A hundred millions at Ottawa for work and wages, and no word for Vancouver, where a thousand jobless men hold out in the post office and the art gallery making a mockery of all ordered government in Canada. No word except the word of folly and ineptitude, to match the stupidity and the impotence of the government at Victoria.
They are going to wear the sit-downers out. They are going to break the deadlock by a nopolicy or forcible-feeble. They are going to twiddle their thumbs and pretend that if they pretend that Vancouver is not there then everything will be all right.
I have an item taken from a prairie paper which is relevant to the situation, reading as follows:
Scores of transients passing through town daily looking for work. Westbound freight trains are the most popular means of transportation. Very few of the men looking for work during the summer season are able to get located as there is little farm work available here. Most of these men are forced to continue their westward trek trudging from town to town.
I suggest to the minister that it should be easily possible to establish direct negotiations with the men in such fashion as to break down this problem into what he described formerly as its component parts. Certain of these men belong to British Columbia, and some scheme should be devised to present them with whatever opportunities there may be for available work. If the minister insists that work is available, it should be possible to present some plan to introduce these men to that work. Most of the evidence before the men is to the effect that no work is available. The evidence is that work

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
is not available for those men who belong in British Columbia and who must look for their employment opportunities in that province.
It should be possible to determine those men who should look for their employment opportunities elsewhere. If there are so many men who should go to Alberta; if there are so many men who should go to Saskatchewan, to Manitoba or to Ontario, it should be possible not only to offer them transportation but to say to them, "We have inquired of the Employment Service of Canada as to opportunities that exist in other provinces; we will see that you get a decent meal when you arrive at these points; if there is work available, you will be advised of it." They should be assured that they will be given every opportunity to work if they are willing to work. If no work is available, they must be assured of some form of food and shelter.
Our experiences in Vancouver have shown us that the alternative to this course is bound to be still more costly. It will be much more costly to send these young men to gaol. Why put them in direct association with hardened criminals of the underworld, with drug addicts, with thieves, with hold-up artists and gangsters? Many young men have told me that after spending two or three months in Oakalla they have been offered propositions by leaders in the underworld. This is a situation that cannot be ignored, and we must reckon with this cost if these men are rushed to gaol or concentration camps.
I was extremely perturbed when I heard the suggestion that force should be used. The acting Postmaster General (Mr. Euler) stated that this situation could not continue indefinitely, that some means should be taken to protect crown property. I know it is important to protect crown property, but it is of greater importance to remember that these men are subjects of the crown and that their welfare should be protected first. If force is used there will be broken heads, there will be blood shed and there will be the danger of lives being lost. That has happened before and it may happen again.
If you attempt to eject 700 men from the Vancouver post office, the resultant property damage will be beyond calculation. Throw in a few tear-gas bombs among 700 men, and the very attempt of such a large mob to escape will result in serious damage. I saw the damage in Hamilton Hall when the police attempted to eject men from that building. We know of the damage that was done to the museum when the police ejected men from that building on a former occasion. The damage will be much greater in the art gallery. If an attempt is made to use force in that
building, within a few minutes valuable works of art may be destroyed. These have been gathered together through the years by endowments from generous citizens. The damage will be absolutely beyond repair.
The alternative is to use some common sense. An effort should be .made to arrive at direct negotiations with these men. The minister will remember that after these men were refused a hearing by the provincial minister of labour, Mr. Pearson, he very courteously received a delegation of five or six of the unemployed. He heard with interest the story as told by the men themselves, and I may tell him that when they returned to the meeting place on Hastings street they told their comrades that the minister had been very decent and they felt they would get a square deal. Just the suggestion that there will be an effort to deal with the situation with some humane understanding means a great deal. I suggest direct negotiations in an understanding and friendly spirit. I suggest a registration of some sort that will determine the various elements and responsibilities in the situation. I suggest a simple plan which, in addition to the offer of transportation, will give these men the assurance that they will be brought closer to whatever work may be available. I can assure the minister that all they are asking is a chance to work, and in the meantime a chance to eat.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour):	Mr. Speaker, I promise the
house that I shall deal briefly with this matter because it has been before us on at least two previous occasions. I have followed carefully what has been said by the hon. members from the city of Vancouver, but they have not set out a situation which differs materially from that which existed when this question was under discussion before. They have directed attention to the fact that thus far these men have maintained themselves in an orderly manner. Short of the fact that they have occupied public buildings, I believe that is substantially true. The hon. member who has just spoken referred in high terms to the character of the majority of the young men who have been involved in this situation. I take no exception to that but, on the other hand, I did take exception before and I do now to the type of leadership which has induced these men to adopt a course of action which I cannot but believe is opposed to their own interests.
I think the house should understand fully that this situation was anticipated to a degree. Before six o'clock my hon. friend referred to the fact that these men are well organized and disciplined. It would not be

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
going too far to say that these men were organized for the purpose of the present demonstration while they were in the forestry conservation camps during the past winter months. That, I think, is a fact which my hon. friend will acknowledge. That is to say, the intention behind the present demonstration in Vancouver was to organize in this way in order to bring about the continuance of the forestry conservation camps during the summer months or to bring about special works projects for the employment of those who had previously been in these camps. That was very clearly the objective of the relief project workers' imion. As a matter of fact, there was published in the Vancouver Sun some days ago an interview in which Mr. Campbell, one of the leaders, admitted this without any hesitation whatsoever.
The original proposal made by the minister of labour of British Columbia was to this effect, that those men who had previously been in the forestry conservation camps and had come to British Columbia from other provinces, should be given transportation back to their homes or places of origin. The minister of labour of British Columbia expressed the view at the same time that it would be possible to absorb the remainder of the single unemployed men in the industries of British Columbia or in such governmental work as might be in operation during the summer months. He referred in particular to the forestry training camp, which will be open in the summer months, and to the placer mining camp, both of these being under the youth training plans which are carried on in cooperation with the dominion government.

speechtext: What were the age limits?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
From eighteen to twentyfive, but exceptions may be made up to the age of thirty years. As my hon. friend is aware, the projects under these youth training plans are agreed upon mutually by the dominion and provincial governments, and there is provision in the agreements whereby admission may be given to those above the age of twenty-five, but generally speaking the age group is from eighteen to twenty-five.
The number of non-residents who are affected at the present time in British Columbia is probably not more than 750. According to my figures the total number of non-resident transients who were in the camps in British Columbia during the winter months was 1,560. We had information to the effect that the deferred pay vouchers which were given to these men on leaving the forestry conservation camps were cashed outside the 
province to the number of 850, which carries with it the implication that some 800 of the 1,560 had gone to other provinces after the forestry camps were closed or after their term of employment in these camps had ceased. That leaves a remainder of about 700 non-resident single unemployed who are now in Vancouver. This brings me to the point where I agree with my hon. friend in his statement before six o'clock that certainly more than fifty per cent of those now involved in this situation are residents of British Columbia. From the beginning the provincial government of British Columbia has taken the position that it should deal with this matter as a question of relief administration within the control of the province, and it has been dealt with in that way. As I have explained to the house before, this government has proceeded upon the basis of consultation and cooperation with the provincial government. In doing that, we are following the course which has been followed in other years.
I should like also to add this with respect to the prospect of employment which lies before these men at the present time. We have it on the basis of our experience last year that some 2,500 of the men who were in the camps previously have not returned to the camps this year. A very careful registration is taken of those who passed through these camps, so when that statement is made we may accept it as being accurate. When one realizes that this was the experience last year, namely that 2,500 men either found employment elsewhere or at any rate did not find it necessary to return to the forestry conservation camps in the winter months, surely we need not assume that there is no opportunity whatever in British Columbia or in the adjoining provinces for absorbing these men.
Then, too, my hon. friend should recognize that the situation to-day is somewhat different from that which he described as existing at the time I was in British Columbia two years ago. On that occasion the transient problem was one which touched rather the opening of these camps during the winter months. The difficulty occurred in the month of November, as he will recall; but the present situation has arisen after these men have had winter employment for varying periods extending from October to the end of April, and certainly in many parts of this country there are men whose employment does not normally extend very much beyond the work that is afforded during the winter months.
My hon. friend suggests that the way to deal with the situation is to provide, through a simple plan, that employment shall be offered to these men in British Columbia. I

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
wish it were as simple as that. I can assure my hon. friend that from one point of view that would be an easy way to deal with the situation. But I would put this question to him: If employment were provided for these men in British Columbia, would that help the solution of the transient problem in that province? His answer would be no. It could not be otherwise. If you create preferred conditions for this particular group of unemployed in one province, certainly you tend to attract to the province others of the transient group in the adjoining province. That has been the experience-

speechtext: Why not do it in the other provinces as well?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
I am coming to that. Clearly, if one were to provide employment for this group in British Columbia, it would be necessary to provide similar employment for this same group in the other provinces. There is no reason why one province should be preferred above another in that respect.
That carries us still further, and I am quite sure that my hon. friend who has just spoken would not overlook this further implication. Is there not an injustice in providing public works for these single unemployed in any province without at the same time finding employment for married men, the heads of families on relief, for war veterans on relief, and for dependents on relief above the age of sixteen years? Surely when one applies reason to this situation, it is evident that you cannot reach a satisfactory solution by conceding to these men, who have adopted this novel and spectacular means of bringing their situation to the attention of this country, opportunities which cannot at the same time be given to other groups of unemployed right across the country.
I should like, in furtherance of what I have just said, to give the house the substance of a telegram which I addressed to the head of the unemployed single men's committee in Vancouver on Friday last. This telegram was in response to a telegram from the single unemployed committee signed by Mr. John Matts, which was as follows:
Two weeks the jobless have been in desperate circumstances. Vain efforts made to seek aid from all authorities. Your representatives turn deaf ear. All we ask is that public works program be started to employ us, that emergency relief be granted. Delay embitters public. Plight unbearable to men. Wire reply.
And this was the reply I sent to that telegram:
Your telegram received this morning. As stated in my previous message the dominion government does not propose to take any action contrary to policy announced by minister of
labour of province of British Columbia. Nonresident single unemployed previously in forestry camps should be advised to accept offer of transportation to homes. Resistance to this proposal chiefly responsible for situation referred to in your telegram. Such men returning to own province will be on same footing as others now unemployed for admission to youth training plans or for such other employment as is available on public works within federal jurisdiction. No works projects will be established exclusively for single unemployed by dominion government in any province but employment on public works will be apportioned as fairly as possible among unemployed married men, returned soldiers and single unemployed as in previous years.
I would submit to my hon. friend who has just spoken that if he were meeting this situation to-day with a full sense of responsibility, I doubt very much whether he would be prepared to go beyond the offer contained in that telegram. In other words, these men will be on the same footing as others who are now unemployed with respect to eligibility for youth training plans or other employment on public works projects. Surely you cannot justify placing them upon any other footing. Undoubtedly they have claims upon our sympathy; no one questions that. There is no member of this house who would not wish that employment might be made readily available for all who are now unemployed in this country. But I do suggest that these men now in Vancouver, who are non-residents of Bhitish Columbia, would be well advised to accept the offer of that province; and certainly every effort will be made to see that they with others who are now unemployed will be given full opportunity for such work as is available on public works projects. My own hope would be that many of those who are now taking part in this demonstration in Vancouver would find that when they really tried to secure employment apart from government projects they would succeed beyond their present expectations.

Departmental administration, $190,670.

speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
This item covers administration, and relates more particularly to the office of the minister, the deputy minister, the secretary, the purchasing agent and the chief architect. When the item was under consideration some time ago, my hon. friend the former Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) inquired about the
Supply-Public Works

appointment of a clerk of tenders. The clerk of tenders who has been appointed is Mr. Rivard, whom he knows. He has been in the service since 1909 and was acting in the capacity of head clerk looking after the correspondence coming to the secretary's office and dealing with the tenders after they had been opened. The civil service commission was asked to reclassify Mr. Rivard as chief clerk, but after consultation the commission decided that the appointment should be made as clerk of tenders. It does not interfere in any way with the rule which has prevailed for many years as to the opening of tenders. Tenders are still opened by the secretary of the department; Mr. Rivard, the clerk of tenders, looks after the correspondence and the tenders before they are opened, and after they are opened he checks up the securities proposed by the tenderers. The appointment and classification have been made by the civil service commission.

This item shows a slight increase from $177,000 to $190,000. The salary deductions which have been restored account for a little over $7,000, so that the increase is not very substantial when that is taken into consideration. However, I should like a little more information in connection with the appointment of this clerk of tenders, particularly as to his duties. As I recall it, before this change, and possibly since, when tenders are invited the tenders were sent to the secretary of the department and were in his custody and control until opened in the manner indicated by the minister. For a considerable number of years there was a vacancy in the office of assistant deputy minister. That vacancy has been filled, and the former secretary who had charge of receiving the tenders is now assistant deputy minister. Are the tenders received by the secretary as formerly? What are the duties of this clerk of tenders? Tenders for work are received over only a part of the year; the estimates go through, and tenders are invited up to the end of the working season; they are dealt with, and the contracts awarded, and then the department is through with tenders so far as dealing with them as tenders is concerned. From that time everything connected with the work comes under the chief architect or his branch, or the engineer's branch, or the accounting branch or some other branch of the department. Why, then, was it necessary to assign a clerk to the duty of looking after tenders? I notice there is an increase from seventy-nine to eighty-one in the number of the staff, which is not material. There appears to have been a change in the number of clerks. Of clerks 
grade 4 there were ten, and now eleven; clerks grade 3, there were eight, and now ten. There is also a decrease in the number of clerks grade 2 from six to five. Perhaps the minister would give us a little more detailed information in connection with the particular appointment to which reference has been made.

There has been practically no change in the duties of Mr. Rivard. He was in the office of the secretary of the department prior to his appointment as clerk of tenders. He had reached the maximum, and his case was submitted to the civil sendee commission in view of the work he had to do and the satisfactory services he had been rendering over a long period of time. The commission inquired into his duties but refused to appoint him as chief clerk, which would have given him a higher salary than that of head clerk; but they said that in view of the duties which he had been performing they felt he should be appointed as clerk of tenders. I do not hesitate to say that this gives him a little higher salary, but his duties are not changed. The practice in dealing with tenders in the department remains unchanged; for the secretary still deals with tenders in the same way as when my hon. friend was in office and, indeed, prior to that time. I repeat, there has been no change except in the designation of the position, giving him a little higher salary on account of the satisfactory services he has rendered. He has been in the service since 1908 or 1909, and the commission were of the opinion that there was justification for the reclassification.
The only way in which the increase could be given him was by reclassifying his office, giving it a baptism and a new name.
That is really what it is.

Item agreed to.
Chief architect's branch-branch administration, $224,460.

I notice what appears to be reorganization of this branch and a substantial increase in the expenditure. For 193738 the amount was $203,000 odd, and this year it is $224,000 odd. There is a new appointment, apparently an additional senior supervising architect, at $4,740. Then there are three supervising engineers of heating, electricity or steel construction: one at $3,960; one at $3,780 and one at $3,600. This makes a total new item of $11,340. I notice that instead of two senior construction architects we now have three. We have one senior mechanical engineer, heating and ventilation,

Supply-Public Works
apparently dispensed with. We come to another item that is inclined to arrest attention for the moment, namely seven senior assistant architects, two at 83,120 and five at $3,000, making a total of $21,240 in connection with this particular item. A little further down we find that the number of assistant architects has been reduced from twelve to eight, making a decrease of four; and immediately following we find a mechanical engineer, heating and ventilation, which is a new appointment, at $2,940. Further down we had last year one architectural specification writer and one assistant architectural specification writer whose services have been dispensed with. Then we have one mechanical draftsman, a new appointment, at $1,560, making an increase in the total of the staff from seventy-eight to eighty-three. Apparently there is some sort of reorganization of the department, and I should be pleased if the minister would outline the scheme of this reorganization and the reasons underlying it.

The increase in the estimates for this year is $20,892, which is made up as follows: The restoration of the five per cent deduction in salaries accounts for $9,000; there are five new positions; there are increases due to promotions, reclassifications and transfers; and there are statutory increases. These give a total of $22,692; but owing to the filling of vacancies at lower rates, there is a decrease amounting to $1,800, giving a net increase of $20,892. The five new positions are: one assistant mechanical engineer, $2,340; three stenographers, grade one; one office boy. These account for $5,340. The other cases my hon. friend has mentioned are reclassifications and transfers. The only new positions are the five I have just indicated.
Were the three supervising engineers of heating, electricity and steel construction promotions? Were they already in the service?
Yes; they are promotions.

The minister might give a little more information with regard to the seven senior assistant architects. Has the policy of the department changed in any way in connection with the architectural services? We have a chief architect, an assistant chief architect, and a new senior supervising architect, and now we have these additional senior assistant architects. Two of these might consist of the architectural specification writer and assistant architectural specification writer, who may have been put in there. That would account for two, if that were so.
I am informed that these seven senior assistant architects appear as result of promotions and transfers. There are no new appointees with the exception of those I have mentioned.
I should think there must be five additional appointees in that total.

The item under consideration has to do with branch administration, and the ex-Minister of Public Works seems very much interested. I wonder if he could tell me something about the Amherst post office which was built in my constituency in 1935, as to why the contract was not awarded to the lowest tenderer.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I have not the book before me-
I have.

-and have not a recollection of every contract that was awarded; but I fancy that if he will ask the minister he will find that it was done on the recommendation of those who were responsible for the action which was taken, and that there was very good reason for it. I do not recall just what it was, but I think he will find the record clean and straight in that connection.

I have had the record
in my possession.

The case to which my hon. friend just referred, and in regard to which he asked a question of the former Minister of Public Works, was covered by the Public Works Construction Act, and under the provisions of that act and the practice developed under it very often preference was given to a local contractor, but at the price of the lowest tender offered to the department. There was a cha.nge of name but not of amount.

I wonder if my hon.
friend would object to that. I thought that explanation was pretty good; that the idea was to give the contract to a local contractor in the town where the work was being performed, at the price of the lowest tender. The public interest was protected; the local interest was served, and the object of the act, which was to give employment in the municipality in which the work was being done, was accomplished.

I wonder if the exMinister of Public Works is familiar with the construction of public buildings. I have gone over and studied the records, and I should like to know just how much the interests of the town of Amherst were served by giving

Supply-Public Works

the contract to a local firm when it was necessary for that firm to bring their key men from outside, and also necessary to import men from other parts of Nova Scotia to do the work. I think I am quite safe in saying that in the construction of that building not more than fifteen or twenty men from the town of Amherst obtained employment. I know something about the construction of buildings, because I was born and brought up in that business. This Public Works Construction Act permitted some strange things. Under this government the contractor who submits the lowest tender gets the job; nobody else gets it. The former government put the Public Works Construction Act into effect, and a friendly firm got the contract. We know that. We might as well talk facts. Everybody in the constituency, whether or not he is in politics, knew what was going on. I know what went on in my constituency, and later on I shall have something more to say about it. These are honest facts I am presenting to-night. The Quebec firm, which was the lowest tenderer on that building, was ignored entirely, and the job was given to a local firm because they were friendly to the government; there was no other reason. Under this Public Works Construction Act it meant nothing but pure politics. We all know that; the people in my constituency know it.
Well, Mr. Chairman, all I have to say to my hon. friend, who seems inclined to inject politics into this discussion at this stage-
I did not inject politics; you did.
I have not injected any politics into anything.
No, not in 1935 or any year from 1930 to 1935.
Who did?
I do not know that anybody did; and I will say this, that if my hon. friend will speak with knowledge-
I do.

*-and accuracy, fairness and justice, he will find that the administration of the Department of Public Works between 1930 and 1935, was as free from politics as it ever was. That is all I have to say in that connection, except that in nearly every case there was pressure-and I think reasonable pressure-to award the con-

tract to a local company. I know there was great objection to contractors coming from the outside, from Quebec or New Brunswick or any other place, into Nova Scotia and doing work there. It was to meet that objection, which appeared reasonable under all the circumstances, that contracts were awarded to local contractors. That was the object. The public interest did not suffer; there was no overexpenditure, and the question of politics did not enter into the matter.
To get back to the item under consideration, has the policy of the department as to the employment of the services of local architects been abandoned, or has the staff been increased or reorganized in order that a larger amount of the work may be done within the department than was formerly the case?
The policy of the department as to acquiring the services of outside architects has not been changed, and the service has not been increased. There has been no change.

I want to reply to the former Minister of Public Works. I can assure him that if it had been a firm that was not friendly to his party, they would not have received much consideration. There is no use in talking about not bringing politics into the matter.
I want to say to my hon. friend at once that I did not know the political complexion of the firm, and do not know it yet.

But those who made
the representation to the hon. member knew it.
There were no representations made along political lines.

The file speaks for
itself; the letters are there to prove what actually took place. I am only interested in knowing why these things happened. They do not happen under this government, so far as I have been able to see in the three years I have been here, whereas under the previous government these things went on not only in Amherst but in other places I could name where this so-called Public Works Construction Act w'as put into force. If that is the way in -which the hon. member handled the money of the taxpayers, I think we should have some explanation of it.

There is one question
I desire to ask, and perhaps it is just as well to ask it under this item as under any other. The minister may not be able to give all the information to-night, but it will be equally

Supply-Public Works
satisfactory if he gives it at some other time. I should like to have the total of the estimates of 1935-36, including the main supplementary estimates and the items under the Public Works Construction Act that were under the control of the public works department. I should also like the total of the estimates for 1936-37 and 1937-38 under the same headings, and for this year as well. Also would the minister state what amount has been expended up to the end of the fiscal year 1938 by the Department of Public Works, and give figures as to the main, supplementary and special items?

The information I have
before me shows that in the main estimates of 1935-36 there was an amount of $14,530,320. in the supplementary estimates, an amount of $2,906,150, and in the further supplementary estimates, a sum of $2,000, making a total appropriation of $17,438,470. Under the Public Works Construction Act there was a sum of $7,892,243, making a grand total of about $24,000,000.
In the main estimates for 1936-37 there was a sum of $13,411,570; in the supplementary estimates, $2,835,700. and in the further supplementary estimates, $12,800, making a total appropriation of $16,260,070. In the special supplementary estimates following the Public Works Construction Act there was a vote of $14,956,585.
In the main estimates of 1937-38 there was a sum of $12,504,420; in the supplementary estimates, a sum of $574,500, making a total of $13,078,920. Then in the special estimates there was a further sum of $12,550,000.
In 1938-39 there is a sum of $12,997,625 in the main estimates, and $13,731,548.57 in the supplementary estimates.

Item agreed to.
Ottawa, maintenance and operation of dominion public buildings and grounds, including rents, repairs, furniture, heating, etc., $2,540,700.

What progress is being made
in Ottawa in connection with improvements undertaken by the government in Confederation square and in connection with the new post office for the city?

The works now contemplated are the supreme court building, the new post office, the widening of the plaza over the tracks near the central station, and the erection of the national memorial. So far as dealing with the city of Ottawa is concerned, there have been no special conversations in regard to the development or beautification of that section. I believe the old Knox church is being taken down.
51952-228J
When are the improvements in Confederation square likely to be completed?
I am informed they will not be completed before next year.
Does the minister refer to the erection of the post office, the erection of the monument, or both?
Both.
Will it take as long as that?

I am informed that the
monument itself will be erected this year, but the terrace to be built around it cannot be completed before next year.
When will the widening of the plaza, or the construction of the bridge, be completed?
The work will be started this year. Plans are almost at the point where tenders may be asked.
Is the minister receiving the whole-hearted cooperation and support of the city of Ottawa with respect to the changes taking place in this city, and particularly in the central portion?
I am informed that they are cooperating with the government and the department.
Are you receiving the cooperation that would tend to a beautification of the city?
Yes.

Is there any hope or prospect of doing something to fire-proof the East block? Every time I have occasion to go there I breathe a sigh of relief when I come out. It is a fire-trap of the worst description, the interior being built entirely of wood. One time when I was on the third floor I got someone to open a trap door I saw there, and I found a passageway possibly four feet by two feet, running the whole length of the corridor. There was a pipe running through this passage; but whether it was for heat or air, I do not know. It was quite obvious that this passageway would act like a chimney in case of fire. If a fire were to start down in the basement, it would be a matter of seconds only before the whole third floor would be a mass of flames.
At one time apparently it was felt advisable to put in so-called fire-doors, which supposedly would be shut in case of fire. This would be all right if the people in the building were all out, but there is one feature of these doors to which I should like to call
Supply-Public Works

attention. They do not open against the wall; they stand open at right angles to the passageway. If there ever were a rush of frightened women, it would be only a matter of seconds before some of them would be shoved behind the door; the door would be closed, the people would pile up against it, and a holocaust would result. It is a reflection upon us here that a building so dangerous should be so close to us.
I realize that these people are generally away at night and there would be little danger in that regard, but I can visualize a fire starting down below and it being only a matter of seconds before it would spread throughout the whole building and many people not be able to get out safely. The officials must be aware of the conditions that exist, and I should like to know if there is any prospect of anything being done?

I agree entirely with the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill). Some time ago a study was made of this building with a view to making it fire-proof. However, the estimate of the cost was so high that it was not thought advisable to proceed with the work. My information is that it would cost $400,000 to make that old building entirely fire-proof. In view of the fact that the government had in mind erecting another building in the vicinity of the Justice building, it was not thought advisable to spend that large amount of money on the East block. I am informed that fire extinguishers have been distributed throughout the building. I am inclined to think, however, that the situation will have to be remedied pretty soon. When the new buildings are completed in a year or two, it is quite likely that many of the departments now in this old building will be removed.

There are three minor repairs which I should like to suggest to the Minister of Public Works. I should like to see an improvement made in the drinking fountains. I should like to see taps installed which would permit a man to take a drink without getting a bath at the same time. This need must be apparent to any hon. member who has occasionally had need of a drink of water in any of these wash-rooms. The other point to which I would direct attention is the air in the basement of this building. That air is positively the worst in the city of Ottawa. I do not know that I have sampled all the air; but I have certainly sampled quite a lot of it in the last ten years, and I do not know of any place where it is worse than in the basement of this building. I always feel

sorry for those who have to work down there, especially in the summer time. The third matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister is the grass in front of this building. We used to have a beautiful sward of grass out there, but to-day it is largely a mass of plantain. I wonder if anything could be done to have grass on that lawm so that the passing wayfarer could look at it and not think this government was going to seed.

I can assure my hon. friend that I shall see the proper officers and have the drinking fountains improved so that there will be no danger of people having to take baths against their will. I shall try at the same time to meet my hon. friend in regard to the condition of the air. In connection with the plantain, as he calls it, may I say that the condition of the grass in certain sections of the grounds may be attributed to the fact that military corps are given the privilege of drilling on the grounds. However, my hon. friend must remember that plantain is very useful for the cure of certain wounds. I learned that in my early days. It may pay us to cultivate and sell it.

While the minister is dealing with minor affairs, perhaps he could give me some information about a matter which may have a certain significance to some of us. I refer to the flag that flies on the parliament buildings. I have noticed that it is flown only five dajrs a week; that it does not appear on the flagstaff on Saturdays and Sundays unless there has been a death in the membership of this house or of the Senate. This building is located opposite the United States legation building which has a flag flying every day in the week. If the flag flying on this building means that the house is in session, perhaps a smaller flag could be used on the other days. Surely a flag should fly seven days of the week on the parliament building of Canada.
My information is that we follow the practice which prevails in England.
Perhaps we can improve on Great Britain.
In connection with the maintenance of the grounds I was under the impression that this duty had been undertaken by the federal district commission.
Yes; that is right.
So my hon. friend would be no longer responsible for the plantain?

No; I am not.

Supply-Public Works

The best piece of grass to be found in the city of Ottawa is west of the West block. The reason for that is that we were given the privilege of using that for an occasional game of baseball. If they would allow us to play down in the front, it would improve the grass immensely.

Item agreed to.
Maintenance and operation of other dominion public buildings and grounds, including rents, repairs, furniture, heating, etc., $3,399,515.

A few minutes ago I asked some questions with regard to the construction work that was going on at the present time in Ottawa. I also asked if the minister was receiving full cooperation from the civic officials in that respect. I was tempted to ask those questions because on several occasions both in this chamber and outside we have heard statements made to the effect that the government is not doing sufficient for the city of Ottawa. Some few weeks ago the minister was good enough to give me certain figures which I shall read to the committee presently.
Personally I do not think the city of Ottawa itself is giving that cooperation which it ought to give the government in its endeavours to make Ottawa a capital worthy of the Dominion of Canada. I think the city itself in the past has been extremely tardy in recognizing Ottawa as being a capital city. It would be exceedingly hard for anyone looking around the city at the present time to discover any civic enterprise that goes to the credit of the city; for anything worth while that is being done is a federal undertaking. Any beautification that has been done has been done at federal expense. Yet whenever I meet people who live here, they always seem to complain that the government is not doing sufficient for the people of the city.
A few weeks ago the minister was good enough to give me a few figures which show what the government has done for Ottawa, and I will put these figures on record. In the past five fiscal years the government have let construction work in this city to the amount of $3,942,632; in the same period it has paid for improvements and repairs, $1,182,416; and for sundry maintenance, $676,679. During the same five years there has been paid out by the government for rents in Ottawa, to property owners within this city, $3,566,678. I shall not give the amount paid in salaries in Ottawa by the government, because I do not think that is necessary. But there is another item of $59,414 which the government paid out in Ottawa in the same period of five years for roads and bridges.
There is another item which I shall give in detail. It shows the expenditures by the federal district commission on improvements in Ottawa in the same five-year period, a total of $1,598,939, made up as follows:

I would go a little further than that. When the government erects valuable buildings in Ottawa they are something more than fine buildings. They are in many respects a monument to the arts and culture of this dominion -expensive buildings like the parliament buildings, for example. We are told that we have exempted government buildings from taxation to the amount of $16,000,000, but it is erroneous to refer to it as it is often referred to in this city. I do not object to the government doing everything possible to make Ottawa worthy of the capital of Canada, but I do feel that in the past the government has not had the whole-hearted cooperation that it should have had from the people of this city. The government are spending vast sums of money in Ottawa, and I do hope that the people of this city will appreciate the money that is being spent here and will give to the government the cooperation that they have a right to expect.

There is a substantial
increase in this item over last year. Last year the amount was $3,295,000, and this year it is $3,399,000 in round figures. Some of the increase is no doubt due to restoration of salary deductions, but I notice there has been an increase in rents from $701,760 last year to $748,860 this year. One would have almost thought that with the new buildings which have been erected we might look forward to a decrease rather than an increase in rents. Perhaps the minister would explain to the
Supply-Public Works

committee this increase in rents, wheth r there has been any additional space taken, and, if so, by what departments.

The increase of $47,100 in rents is due to the following: forty-three new leases; seven increases in existing leases; forty-nine decreases in existing leases; increase in allotment for probable requirements, from $15,000 to $20,000; increase in allotment for probable requirements for National Defence, from $50,000 to $73,000. There is a net increase of $19,127 as regards the forty-three new leases, and there is an allotment of $23,000 for probable requirements for National Defence.

No; I would not ask for those details. It seems a little strange that each year we are putting up new public buildings throughout the dominion to accommodate the services, and moving them in; yet at the same time our rents are increasing. It is the same old problem.

I noticed the other day the deputy minister made a dignified protest to the city with regard to the possible erection of a gas station on the corner of Lyon and Wellington street. I do not think the dominion government owns any of the land on the south side of Wellington street, but I wonder whether there exists any design accepted by the city, perhaps approved by the government, which will govern the erection of the buildings which will gradually be built along the south side of Wellington street opposite what will be a magnificent facade of dominion government buildings on the north side.

We have no understanding with the city of Ottawa as to the south side of Wellington street, but the letter of the deputy minister has been very well and favourably received by the board of trade. At the present time there are no plans supplying any detail as to the future development of the south side of Wellington street.

none of it?

And the supreme court building will be next to the roadway just beyond the justice building?
Yes.
Will the chimney of the heating plant be in the way?
I expect the architects have been considering doing away with the chimney somehow in order that it shall not interfere with the fine view that will be presented when the supreme court is there.

Is the increase due to
