What is the nature of
the improvements to Rideau Hall?
To provide for the replacement of two greenhouses, and alterations to Rideau Lodge at the entrance of the front driveway, requested by Colonel Mackenzie of government house.
What is the nature of the improvements and repairs to the dominion building in Toronto?

Painting of the exterior of the building, and the interior decorating of the five floors of the west wing, basement and warehouse portion.

Supply-Public Works
That is not the old post office building, is it?
That is the customs house.
The new customs building.

Item agreed to.
Manitoba-
Dominion public buildings-improvements and repairs, $40,000.
Steinbach-public building, $3,000.

In connection with the new public buildings to be constructed in Ottawa-I speak particularly about the new post office and the supreme court building- what type of stone is mentioned in the specifications for these buildings?

The specifications are not completed yet, but for the supreme court building it will be stone to match the Justice and Confederation buildings. For the post office it is granite or limestone, but the specifications have not yet been drawn up.

My information is that in the contract or plan being prepared for the post office building Canadian limestone or Canadian granite is specified, alternate tenders. That applies only to two provinces where they can quarry that kind of stone; it does not apply to my province, which supplied the Wallace sandstone in this building, the Confederation building and several other buildings in Ottawa. My information further is that the reason Wallace sandstone has not been included in the specifications is the fact that they can deliver it here cheaper than any other stone. I should like to have some information on that point.

The government has been consulting a town-planning architect of great reputation, Mr. Greber, and I am informed he suggests that the post office should be built of granite or limestone to match the monument, the base of which will be of granite. The Chateau Laurier and the station are also of light-coloured stone.

If my information is correct, this and other governments have followed the policy of having all these buildings as nearly uniform in appearance as possible. I think we have rather gone astray in connection with the Bank of Canada, which was built of granite. Wallace sandstone is produced in the constituency which I have the honour to represent; but as a matter of fact very little labour is spent upon it in that constituency, because most of the stone is shipped to Quebec where it is turned out in its finished state.
I know that the company in my constituency does not expect all the business; but I submit that at least it should be recognized when the specifications are being prepared, and I know that we have not been recognized in the post office specifications. In connection with the specifications for the construction of the Supreme Court building, I think the constituency I represent should be given some consideration, and I should like to have a definite statement from the minister in that regard.
My information is that up to the present Wallace sandstone has been used extensively in the city of Ottawa.
In the past, yes.
Well, my hon. friend should not despair.

I wish to be fair in this matter; but I would ask the minister, Why is it that Wallace sandstone was used in the past? It was a matter of price; that is all. Now, the taxpayers are paying for all these buildings, and if the department is going to discriminate against a particular company because it can supply stone cheaper than it can be procured elsewhere, that is not just and fair to all the producers in Canada. All I ask is that we be given a chance to bid. If, after the tenders are in, there is an objection to using sandstone, then I have nothing further to say; but as the representative of the constituency of Cumberland I feel I ought to bring this matter to the attention of the minister. I should like to have a definite statement as to what is to be used in the Supreme Court building. I understand that the designs are being prepared by a Montreal architect, and I would point out that seventy-five per cent of the labour spent on Wallace sandstone is spent in Quebec because the stone is shipped to that province in the rough state. After all, Ottawa is in one province, and I submit that we should have some consideration in connection with all these millions that are being expended here. I do not think I am unfair in making this request.
What sandstone was used in the trimmings of the Confederation and the Justice buildings?
Wallace sandstone. That was used also in the parliament building and the national research building.

I think my hon. friend will find that other dealers in stone complain that Wallace sandstone has been getting too much of a show in Ottawa. That has been the complaint in the past.
Supply-Public Works
On account of the price; that is the only reason.
Not on account of the price. As I recall it, the sound practice of the Public Works department is not to specify any particular kind of stone, brick, hardware or other material.
You are wrong; read the specifications.
Perhaps I do not know as much about it as my hon. friend does, but the reason for that practice is that if you specify a particular kind of stone or granite you give a preference.
I do not ask that.

I am not concerned with what the hon. gentleman is asking. I say that the reason for not specifying a particular kind of stone is as I have indicated, and it is a sound one, because if they specified granite my hon. friend would be complaining that they should specify Wallace sandstone. For that reason, therefore, the specifications are left open.
They are not left open.
They are.
Well, read them.
They are left open to a large extent
Oh, no.

-in order that the
manufacturers of different classes of material will all have a chance to tender.

My hon. friend is
wrong.

I will ask the minister if that is not the settled policy of the department. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman is trying to qualify for Minister of Public Works, but he seems to display a remarkable amount of inaccuracy in his information.

I am not an old man; but I think I have almost as good a knowledge of this matter as some of those who have been in the office of the Minister of Public Works, and I do not care whether it is in connection with civil engineering, or anything else. If an engineer can design a building, I can build one, and that is more than some engineers can do. I am not saying anything against the hon. member, but he is wrong. He has not read the specifications for the new post

office, and I can tell him what is contained in them. They provide for Canadian limestone or granite.
Canadian limestone leaves it open to any province that has limestone.
And how many provinces have limestone?

Quebec, Ontario and
Manitoba.

I respect the Ontario
members, but I want to read an article that appeared in the Engineering and Contract Record. It is headed:
Request Use of Ontario Stone in Ottawa Buildings.
Ontario cut stone contractors have circularized Ontario federal members seeking their support for Ontario Queenston or Rama limestone in the construction of dominion government buildings at Ottawa. There is no cut stone from an Ontario quarry in any of the major federal buildings in Ottawa, the brief states. The buildings have all been built with cut stone from the sandstone quarries of the maritime provinces or with granite from Quebec, with the exception of the Hunter building which is of brick trimmed with Tyndall limestone from Manitoba. The brief is signed by Robert Sharp, Hamilton, and George W. Ritchie, Toronto, on behalf of ten different cut stone contractors, including two firms in Ottawa, two in Hamilton, one in London and five in Toronto.
All that I ask is that the company in my constituency be given an opportunity to tender. They are not being given that opportunity in the specifications prepared for the post office, and I am making this plea on their behalf. As regards Canadian limestone, so far as Manitoba is concerned, we might as well forget it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member, but his remarks all have reference to buildings in the city of Ottawa. We have passed that item and are now discussing buildings in Manitoba.

This is the first time I have spoken in the House of Commons although I have been here three sessions. I do not appreciate being ruled out of order. I am talking about dominion public buildings, no matter in what province they are situated. The particular buildings to which I am now referring are in the city of Ottawa. I do not appreciate the fact that I am called out of order-
Mr. STEWAfRT: Mr. Chairman, is this hon. member to defy the authority of the chair?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I did not call the hon. member out of order; I pointed out to him- will he please resume his seat?

Supply-Public Works
I was bora in the country, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. member please resume his seat?
-so you will have to pardon me.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am trying to be fair to the hon. member, but he has been talking about certain stone used in certain federal buildings in the city of Ottawa. I pointed out to him that those items had passed, and that the committee were now considering buildings in the province of Manitoba.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I shall have to submit to your ruling. I did not know that it made any difference, when we were talking about dominion public buildings, whether they were in Manitoba or in any other part of the country, because after all we are speaking about Canada, and if my memory serves me aright all these provinces are in Canada. I am not trying to be unfair; I want to be reasonable, but I do feel that this company should be given an opportunity to tender on the post office building, and they have not been given that chance. I think I should have some explanation. I am told they have been eliminated on account of the fact that they can deliver the stone here more cheaply than any other firm. That is the whole story. Who are paying for these buildings? They are paid for by the taxpayers of the country. Are we going to put up buildings regardless of cost just because certain members make representations that certain stone should be used? I do not think we should.

My hon. friend is not fair when he says certain members have been making representations. In regard to the post office building that is to be put up here, the quality of the stone has been indicated by the town-planning architect who was consulted by the government. It is on his advice alone that it has been stated that the stone for the post office should be rather granite or limestone. There has been no other representation made in that regard.
Is that in keeping with the policy which was laid down for these improvements in Ottawa? I do not think it is.
It is in keeping with the program for the beautification of Ottawa.
My understanding was that the buildings should be uniform in appearance.
In that section, at least.

Why should an architect have any authority to say what stone is going to be used? It is not the quality of the stone that is in question, because we can see it here in this building. I do not see why an architect should take away any authority from the government.

He is not taking any
authority away from the government. The government consulted him, and it is on his advice that this kind of stone has been chosen for the post office, because it is a light-coloured stone. That was the suggestion of the architect whom we consulted, and that is the only reason for this decision. There was no intention in the world to exclude the quarries of the province which my hon. friend represents in this house.

Well, as I said before, I do not want to be unfair; but the fact that the stone is of a light colour does not seem to me to be a very strong argument as to why it should be used. The quality of Wallace sandstone is shown in all these buildings here in Ottawa, and that stone has been used because of the price at which it can be delivered here. We built the Bank of Canada building of granite; but that will not contribute to the improvement of Wellington street, because there we shall have a building that will stand by itself and will not correspond with any other building. All I ask is that the Wallace quarries be given a chance to tender. Then, if the government does not want their stone, all right; but they have been given no opportunity to tender. They have been entirely eliminated. All I am asking, is that they be given an opportunity, and I think any company doing business in Canada to-day should be given an opportunity to tender. Then, if the government or the architect in charge does not consider that the stone is of the right quality or the right colour, that is all there is to it. We have many buildings here of the same colour, the Confederation building, the East and West blocks and this parliament building, and I have never heard anyone say anything against the colour. Surely we must consider the quality before the colour.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Carried.
It is not carried with my consent.

Item agreed to.
Supply-Public Works

Alberta-
Dominion public buildings-improvements and repairs, $40,000.
Peace River-public building, $36,000.
What is the $36,000 for in Peace River? Is that a new building; and, if so, where is it to be constructed?
That is a new building. This amount has been appearing in the estimates for a couple of years, but we have experienced some difficulty as to the site where that public building is to be erected.
Then as yet it has not been decided where the building is to be erected?
No.
What is to be the nature of the building?	.
It is for a post office.

Item agreed to.
British Columbia-
Dominion public buildings-improvements and repairs, $50,000.
Kelowna-public building, $10,000.
Powell River-public building, $58,000.
Prince Rupert-public building, $170,000.

I notice this vote is described as having to do with public buildings, but of course it means post offices. Of these there are three: one at Kelowna, where the cost apparently is about $60,000; one at Powell River, costing $58,000-and I know that is lcng overdue-and another at Prince Rupert, costing $170,000. That also is overdue. I wonder, however, what has become of the vote for the post office in the city of Alberni, which, so far as age goes, antedates these others by a good many years. It was a settlement some ten or twelve years before confederation, while these others are comparatively of mushroom growth. During the years of the depression, while we were fully aware of the need for a proper building there, we put forward no claim, knowing the need for economy on the part of the government; but as things got better, last year and the year before, we thought we would put forward our modest claim. It happened to be opportune to have one of the head men of the Post Office Department visit Alberni. He walked into the post office and remarked that the accommodation was entirely inadequate for the business done.
Some reference was made to-night with regard to a revote for a public building because the department were not able to get a site. As the minister is aware, the city of Alberni voted the government one of the best lots in the city, free of all charge, for the construction of this post office. The cost was very moderate; if I remember aright we asked that the government spend only some $17,000. That was the estimated cost, without paying anything for a site. The total cost of these other three buildings to which I have referred is $288,000, and an additional $17,000 would not have been a very great addition to that amount. There is no question that this post office building is needed, with the increase in the population of the city, and the business done there would fully justify it; so would the post office revenue. Would the minister indicate first what has become of the item that was put in for this vote, and also whether or not he can hold out any prospect of its being included in further supplementaries ?

I am afraid this year it will be impossible to meet the request of the hon. member. The Minister of Finance has intimated to all ministers that he does not propose to introduce further supplementary estimates. The only thing I can say to the hon. member is that his project has taken the same route as one I proposed for my own constituency. I refer to a site which for a number of years has existed in one of the small towns in my riding. Until this time, however, it has been impossible to erect a public builidng on it. This year I tried to use all my power with the Minister of Finance, but I could not succeed. I am afraid my case is similar to that of the hon. member. May I point out to him, however, that he has my word that I shall keep the two matters in mind. The site at St. Ours was bought more than fifteen years ago, but the building has not yet been erected. I shall keep the two matters together, and when I feel that my power and influence is strong enough to have the building erected at St. Ours, I shall remember the claim of the hon. member.
I thank the minister. But if it would meet the situation, I would not object if he were to cut out the vote for Kelowna for this year.
Item agreed to.

Supply-Public Works
Generally-Dominion immigration buildings- repairs, improvements, etc., $35,000.
The amount seems to be exactly the same as last year. Was last year's vote expended, or is this a re vote?
This is a maintenance vote for repairs and renewals.

How much was spent
last year?

Practically the whole of
it, I am informed.

Item agreed to.
National monument on Connaught place, $150,000.
Would the minister give some information as to the total cost of the work, whether contracts have been awarded, when they are likely to be completed and so on?

The contract for the base of the monument has been awarded to the Cape construction company of Montreal. They are ready to start work as soon as we have disposed of the old post office. The granite is being cut and prepared, and they are ready to begin work on the foundation.
What is the amount of the contract?

Where will the centre
of the monument be? Will it be on the centre line of Sparks and Elgin streets?
It is a little west of the site of the post office which is being demolished.
I suppose there is cellarage under the old post office?
Yes.
And considerable foundation work will have to be done where the cellarage existed?
No; it is west of that point.
It will miss the post office?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Chief engineer's branch-Branch administration, $210,880.

The details indicate that there is some reorganization or rearrangement. I note particularly that there are three
additional superintending engineers at $4,980 each, and an increase in the number of clerks, the total number being increased from sixty-three to seventy-three. The total expenditure, including the restoration of salary deductions, amounts to $210,880, as against $172,541 for the last fiscal year. What is involved in the reorganization? Where are the three superintending engineers located? Are there any new divisions, and what necessitated the appointment of the additional engineers?

The increase shown is due, first, to the restoration of the five per cent deduction. That factor accounts for $6,969. There are ten new positions, and there are increases due to promotions and statutory increases. The new positions relate to the appointment of three superintending engineers, involving an amount of $14,940. These engineers have been promoted to Ottawa. Mr. Goodspeed was formerly in Winnipeg and Mr. Sabourin was in Quebec city. It was thought advisable to bring to the Ottawa office men who had experience in the various engineering districts of the country, so that they would be more familiar with the districts of which they are in charge. It is because of that fact they have been called to Ottawa to form a sort of board to advise the chief engineer as to what would be necessary, useful or practical in the various districts of Canada. There is one in Ottawa charged particularly with supervising recommendations coming from Ontario. One was brought from Winnipeg to advise us as to the needs of the western provinces, and the third was brought from Quebec to advise as to the requirements of that province as a whole. No new appointments have been made, the men being brought to Ottawa from the outside offices. The other cases are all promotions. The salaries of these different engineers total $27,420.

Will the bringing in of
these engineers involve the appointment of other engineers at a later date to do their work?

It is only a question of
promotion from junior rank to a senior position. The junior positions were filled by the civil service commission.

The district engineer
who was at Winnipeg has been promoted to superintending engineer and brought to Ottawa. Is the work of the Winnipeg district now being done by the man who was his assistant?

I am informed that in the reorganization the engineer at Charlottetown
Supply-Public Works

was promoted to the position in Winnipeg. The only new appointments that have been made by the civil service commission are those at the bottom of the list, the junior positions.

Did I understand the
minister to say that these engineers will now be located at Ottawa and will form a board to advise the chief engineer?
Yes.

That is a new feature.
As I recall it, these engineers came in from the outside perhaps once or twice a year and consulted with the chief engineer. Now they are to be located permanently at Ottawa. In addition to the chief engineer and assistant chief engineer there will be three superintending engineers.

I am informed that these
positions have not been created. The engineers who previously made up this board have been retired. I am informed that there was a board in Ottawa which dealt with the same problem with which these supervising engineers will have to deal.

Item agreed to.
Engineering, including salaries of engineers, clerks, etc., $515,245.
Will the minister explain the increase?

There is a gross increase
of $25,000, made up as follows:
Return of five per cent deduction, $17,000.
Two new positions, $3,480.
Statutory increases, $4,200.
There is a decrease of $13,920 due to filling vacancies at lower rates and the abolition of the position of district engineer, grade 1. This leaves a net balance of about $11,000. The new positions are an assistant engineer for the Fort William and Port Arthur district, which is to be filled by promotion, and one stenographer at Charlottetown. The position at Three Rivers has been abolished, the work of that district being divided between Montreal and Quebec.
There is only one additional engineer being appointed at Port Arthur and Fort William?
Just one.

Item agreed to.
Dredging-Maritime provinces, $375,000.
Would the minister explain the substantial increase?

This amount of $375,000 is required to carry out dredging operations in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island by departmental plant, and to provide for the repair and maintenance of this plant during the fiscal year.
I do not suppose the minister has laid out a program for this work.
A tentative program only.
The principal increase seems to be in the work program, from $22,000 to $45,815. There is also an increase in new plant. What new plant is contemplated?
I am informed that some pontoons are required for dredge No. 12 and also a scow for dredge No. 13.

Item agreed to.
Dredging-Ontario and Quebec, $326,700.
What is the work to be carried on in Ontario under this item?

This amount is made up
as follows:
Permanent staff	$ 7,620
Wages	 70,482
Maintenance and operation	 91,458
New Plant	 10,005
Contract and day labour works, inspection and contingencies and to supplement above	allotments. 147,135

The officers intimate that it is impossible to tell definitely what repairs will be required during the year, and the amount of wages to be paid depends on the length of the operating season, which is governed by weather conditions. No list has been prepared of the works to be undertaken.
What are the particulars of the new plant?
There are two new 40 cubic yard dump scows for dredge No. 126 at $6,670, and one new 40 cubic yard dump scow for dredge No. 127, at $3,335, or a total of $10,005.

Item agreed to.
Dredging-Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, $110,000.

This and the previous
item link together several provinces. Item No 302 covers Ontario and Quebec; and item No. 303, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Apparently the minister is not prepared to treat each province separately. I have no objection to the item, but I think it would be better if we had each province separate.

Supply-Public Works

The suggestion of my hon. friend no doubt has some merit, but the vote has been carried in this way for a number of years and has worked out satisfactorily. Each province is considered on its merits, and the amounts spent in each province are practically equal. Probably the reason for having the provinces coupled together was that there would be fewer items of a similar kind in the estimates.

I notice there is an increase for total salaries and wages in every province except the three prairie provinces, where there is a reduction in that item. Is this on account of a reduction in salaries and wages or a reduction in staff?
I am informed that there is no reduction at all in salaries and wages.
Then the reduction of 82,382 must be due to a reduction in staff?
I am informed that it is due to not so many dredges being in commission.
Where is the $46,000 new plant in the prairie provinces to be located?
That is for a new tug on lake Winnipeg, the old one having been condemned.

Item agreed to.
Maintenance and operation of graving docks, locks and dams, etc.-Champlain graving dock, $69,000.
May I ask if graving docks are for the use of Public Works boats, or does the item also concern the Department of Transport?

The graving dock can be
used by any vessel.
As well as by Public Works vessels?
Yes.
Is there any revenue from the public use of the dock?
There is a regular schedule of tolls, regulated by order in council.
Does the public use the dock to any extent? Is there a considerable revenue?
Yes.
Why is the dock at Saint John, New Brunswick, not in this list also?
The Saint John dock is a subsidized dry dock.
What does the revenue amount to?
The revenue for 1936-37 was $27,344, and the total revenue since 1921-22 has been $601,863.

Item agreed to.
Esquimalt graving dock, $83,000.
What is the revenue at Esquimalt?
In 1936-37 fifty-three vessels were docked there, and the revenue was $36,156. The total revenue since 1926-27 amounts to $318,223.36.

Item agreed to.
Lome graving dock, $40,000.
Where is this dock?
It is at Lauzon, opposite Quebec.

Item agreed to.
Maintenance and operation of locks and dams, $62,800.
Has this item to do with the Rideau canal?

No; that is under the Department of Transport. This appropriation is to provide for the operation and maintenance of various locks and dams formerly charged to several general appropriations. The names of the dams are as follows: Riviere du Lievre lock and dam; French river dam; Latchford dam on Montreal river; St. Andrews lock and dam; Cowan dam; Okanagan dam at Penticton, storage dams on the Ottawa river, Quinze and Timiskaming.

Item agreed to.
Maintenance and operation of snagboats, $41,000.

This may not be the appropriate item, but I do not know any other. Would the minister deal with Ripple rock under this item? I noticed in the paper that there was to be a sum put in the supplementary estimates to survey it, but my impression was that it was thoroughly surveyed some years ago and the method for getting rid of it settled.
It is a big job, likely to cost some $400,000.

I understand the department is informed as to the cost of disposing of that obstacle to navigation, and that it would be a costly proposition. We have not provided for that work this year. As far as
Supply-Public Works

investigation is concerned, I am informed by the officers of the department that they have practically all the information they require.
That is obtained by some officials appointed by the government?
Yes.
My impression is, speaking from a rather treacherous memory, that the cost would not be very great, I think about $125,000.
Nearer half a million.
It is vague in my mind, but I remember having seen some such report as my hon. friend speaks of, but it did not emanate from the department; it came from some other source.

There was a notice in the Vancouver paper that information had been given out from Ottawa that a sum of $5,000 was going to be voted for a survey, and my information is that Mr. Forde, the district engineer, or someone under him, carried out a survey some years ago, and decided that the only practical way to do the work was to run a tunnel from the side under the bed of the Narrows-they had to go some ninety feet deep-and then go up under the rock and blow it up. The cost was estimated at somewhere around $125,000. There seems to be a difference between what is reported in the paper and the minister's statement. The minister says they have all the information they need.

I am informed that a board of engineers was appointed and they had a public hearing some years ago. I am informed also that a request was made to the department to provide a further sum to make a survey, but we did not comply with that request because we felt we had all the information required. It was only a case of deciding whether or not we would do the work.
And it has been decided not to do it this year?
Not this year.

Item agreed to.
Maintenance and operation of roads and bridges-Burlington channel bridge, $16,000.
Why are six additional bridge men necessary?
I am informed that the staff has not been increased, but that some temporary employees have been made permanent.
The list on page 185 of the estimates shows six more men for 1938-39 than for 1937-38.
As temporary employees their names do not appear in the estimates.
Surely it does not take eleven men to operate the Burlington bridge.
I notice that last year the temporary assistance was $4,320, and this year it is $500. Is the explanation that those temporary assistants have been appointed permanently?
These employees were paid as temporary, and now they are being made permanent. The number of men is the same; there has been no increase.
Are they appointed by the civil service commission?
Yes.
Does that mean that eleven men are employed to operate the Burlington bridge?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Kingston, La Salle causeway, $10,500.
I notice there is $2,274 for temporary assistance. The men on the Burlington bridge are made permanent. Why should these men at Kingtson be temporary?
I am informed that these men are not particularly looking after the bridge but rather are looking after the piece of land there.
There is no land around the La Salle bridge.
I should like to know the duties of these men. Surely the government does not keep two men to look after that land on La Salle causeway. There is no land there to speak of.
Is there a wharf, or some part of the causeway used for landing of boats? I have noticed them tied up there.
I think that would be part of the duties of these temporary men.
I was not sure whether that was operated by the Public Works department or the Department of Marine.

We look after the maintenance, repairs and operation of the combined roadway, wharves and bridges over the

Supply-Public Works
Cataraqui river at Kingston. I regret very much that I am not in a position to give a satisfactory answer to my hon. friend. I will undertake to supply that information on some other occasion when dealing with the estimates. There is still a good deal to* be disposed of and I will supply that information, if the hon. member does not object to passing this item.

Item agreed to.
Ottawa, bridges and approaches, $26,200.
To what bridges around Ottawa does this refer?
The Chaudiere, the Laurier avenue and the union bridges.
There seems to be a substantial increase in the amount to be expended this year. Where is it proposed to make this increased expenditure?
It is to pave the union bridge.

Item agreed to.
Nova Scotia-
Essential undertakings-Little Anse-breakwater reconstruction, $43,400.
Malagash-wharf improvements, $19,000.
New Harbour-breakwater repairs, $8,200.
Harbours and rivers generally-for maintenance of services, no new works to be undertaken, $250,000.
Why is this amount of $43,400 required in connection with Little Anse breakwater reconstruction?

This is required to provide for the reconstruction of the cribwork reinforcing block, 210 feet by 20 feet located on the harbour side of the breakwater. Attention is directed to the necessity of this work by district engineer Cox, who reports that the section of work to be rebuilt is badly damaged by action of the teredo, and in its present weakened condition is liable to be washed away at any time.
Will the minister explain the item of $19,000 for Malagash.

This is required to provide for encasing the outer end of the public wharf with steel sheet piling, placing filling between the existing cribwork and proposed piling and laying a reinforced concrete deck four inches thick. Attention is directed to the necessity of the proposed work by the district engineer, who reports that this structure is in a bad condition owing to the ravages of sea worms. He reports also that pile
work will not be as suitable as sheet steel piling, which will withstand to. a greater degree the ice shoves at this place and will also better support the Malagash salt company's conveyer and the structure they intend to erect to house machinery of considerable weight.
The principal traffic over the wharf is salt?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
